title: A microbial platform for selective biosynthesis of monoterpene esters

paper_content.abstract: Reconstructing the precise biosynthesis of structurally complex natural esters, such as monoterpene esters, in engineered microbes remains a major challenge, owing to the limited repertoire of highly selective alcohol acyltransferases and the lack of compatible pathway modularity. Here, we establish a dual-substrate microbial platform to profile the activities of alcohol acyltransferase (AAT) to synthesize three distinct classes of monoterpene esters: monoterpenyl esters, monoterpenoate esters, and monoterpenyl monoterpenoate esters, enabling access to both natural and non-natural monoterpene ester biosynthetic pathways. Through structure-guided critical residue engineering and dual-substrate molar ratio tuning, we achieve selective biosynthesis of >C2 acyl-CoA-derived monoterpene esters, despite competing intracellular acetyl-CoA. Coculture engineering further redistributed metabolic fluxes between acyl-CoA and alcohol precursors, yielding 11.50 g/L linalyl acetate and 3.16 g/L geranyl butyrate in 1-L bioreactor. This study expands the biosynthetic space of monoterpene esters and provides a versatile strategy to control AAT selectivity, offering a plug-and-play, scalable framework for ester biomanufacturing.
paper_content.introduction:
Natural esters, primarily recognized as either volatile compounds responsible for fruity and floral aromas or as acylated derivatives of complex natural products, are ubiquitous in flowers, traditional fermented foods, and medicinal plants (e.g., rose1, 2, wine3, Baijiu4, Strychnos nux-vomica5, etc). Since the term "ester" was first introduced in 1848 by German chemist Leopold Gmelin to describe the condensation product of acids and alcohols6, natural esters have garnered extensive attention due to their structural diversity, sensory importance, and biosynthetic complexity. Their entire biosynthesis involves intricate modular biosynthetic pathways distributed across microbial and plant cellular systems4, 7. Engineering microbes to synthesize these esters presents considerable challenges, particularly in achieving controlled and efficient biosynthetic pathways. A primary hurdle is the unclear specificity and selectivity of enzymes at critical metabolic junctions8. Natural ester intracellular biosynthesis is predominantly mediated by alcohol acyltransferases (AATs), which catalyze the esterification of acyl-CoAs and alcohols9. However, the inherent broad substrate promiscuities of AATs for both donor dimensions typically form multiple ester products instead of the desired singular compound in engineered microbial or natural systems10. Furthermore, intracellular ester biosynthesis relies heavily on the availability of dual substrates—acyl-CoAs and alcohols—whose availability is regulated by primary or secondary metabolic networks11, 12, such as glycolysis, citric acid cycle, fatty acid biosynthesis/degradation, amino acid biosynthesis/degradation, mevalonate pathway, polyketide biosynthesis, etc. Typically, the imbalance or limitation in precursor supply from these upstream biosynthetic pathways, whether in nature or engineered hosts, can critically hinder AAT-driven ester formation, thereby reducing product formation specificity and efficiency.

Over the past two decades, advancements in metabolic engineering have significantly facilitated microbial design, enabling AAT-mediated biosynthesis of structurally diverse esters using engineered microbes consuming glucose, glycerol, or ethanol13-16. Ester biosynthesis approaches in engineered microbes have involved esterification of short-chain fatty alcohols (SCFAlcs) with various acyl-CoAs by AATs17, optimization of enzyme specificity through substrate-tunnel engineering to reduce intermediate-derived by-product formation7, and coculture strategies to minimize cellular metabolic burdens and substrate promiscuity by dissecting the entire biosynthetic pathway and temporally cascade inoculations18. Despite these progressions, precision ester biosynthesis in engineered microbes remains constrained by insufficiently characterized biocatalytic modules of AATs and the incompatibility of upstream metabolic pathways17, 19-21.

Monoterpene esters (MEs), a highly valuable class of natural products extensively applied as flavors, fragrances, food additives, cosmetic ingredients, advanced biofuels, insecticides, etc (Supplementary Tables 1-2, Supplementary Data 1)9, 22-26, exemplify these constraints in microbial biosynthesis. Structurally, MEs originate primarily from the esterifying reactions between monoterpenols (MTs) and acyl donors, or between alcohols and monoterpenoic acid (MTa)-derived acyl-CoAs (Fig. 1). However, current engineered microbial systems produce a narrow range of MEs, primarily derived from acetyl-CoA27, including geranyl acetate (GAC)28, neryl acetate29, and perilla acetate30. Controlling the specificity of ME biosynthesis critically depends on the characterization and development of highly selective AATs capable of utilizing C>2 acyl-CoAs amid high intracellular acetyl-CoA concentrations. Moreover, as both monoterpenes and acyl-CoAs share acetyl-CoA as a common precursor, finely tuning the molar ratio and compatibility of metabolic fluxes toward alcohol and acyl-CoA biosynthesis is essential to achieve high specificity and titer of ME in engineered microbes.

Here, we develop a dual-substrate microbial platform to profile the catalytic activities of AATs in engineered Escherichia coli, synthesizing three distinct classes of MEs: Monoterpenyl Esters (MTEs), Monoterpenoate Esters (MTaEs), and Monoterpenyl Monoterpenoate Esters (MtMtaEs) (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1). By bioconverting MTs or MTas individually with their pairing substrates, we generate 64 MTEs, 3 MTaEs, and 4 MtMtaEs, a type of underexplored monoterpene dimeric esters with four isoprene units. This comprehensive profiling enables the identification of AAT exhibiting either broad or highly specific dual-substrate acceptance patterns for both alcohols and acyl-CoAs. Structure-guided engineering of the critical residue in AATs under adjusted acyl-CoA-to-alcohol molar ratios efficiently mitigated substrate specificity imbalances, in particular between acetyl-CoA and butyryl-CoA, allowing the precise biosynthesis of a variety of MEs and aromatic esters with >99% selectivity. Leveraging a modular coculture strategy to enhance dual-substrate availability and compatibility, we demonstrate the de novo biosynthesis of 7 MTEs using an E. coli-E. coli consortium with MT as the bridging molecule, achieving a titer exceeding 11 g/L for one MTE in a 1-liter bioreactor. This study highlights the advantages of AAT-mediated ME biosynthesis and provides a versatile framework for selective ester biosynthesis in engineered microbes, significantly enhancing the diversity, substrate specificity, and pathway modularity.
paper_content.results:
Biosynthesis of monoterpenoate esters

To explore the diversity of MTE biosynthesis using various sourced AATs, the acid donor should be available as CoA-activated molecules (Fig. 2a). We selected a butyrate-acetoacetate CoA-transferase from Clostridium acetobutylicum (CaBACT) for activating short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) into acyl-CoAs31. The selection of the 14 AATs from bacteria, yeast, and plant was based on the previously reported studies, indicating their enzymatic activity in forming acetate-based MTEs7, 19, 32, 33. The phylogenetic analysis reveals the evolutionary divergence and conservation among the amino acid sequences of AATs (Fig. 2b and 2c, Supplementary Fig. 2). The close clustering of LiAAT4, FvAAT, and FaAAT in the phylogenetic tree suggests that these AATs may share a similar dual-substrate specificity. Using engineered E. coli strains expressing individual AATs with or without CaBACT, we conducted esterification reactions by feeding selected MTs and carboxylic acids. The resulting MTEs were captured into the organic phase of culture during fermentation and analyzed by GC-MS (Supplementary Fig. 3). Characteristic ester bond fragmentation patterns were observed, with monoterpenols such as geraniol, nerol, and lavandulol forming base ions at m/z = 69 and linalool at m/z = 93 due to its distinct allylic rearrangement (Supplementary Table 3)34. Characteristic m/z fragments (43, 57, 71, 85) derived from C2-C5 SCFAs enabled unambiguous MTE identification, even without NIST MS references (Supplementary Data 2). Four representative AATs, including FvAAT, FaAAT, LiAAT4, and ScAAT1, were characterized for their activities with acetyl-CoA, propionyl-CoA, and valeryl-CoA. FvAAT, FaAAT, and LiAAT4 displayed broad catalytic activity, capable of accepting C2-C5 acyl donors and diverse MTs (Fig. 2d, Supplementary Figs. 4-25). Among all the validated AATs, LiAAT4 and ScAAT1 showed catalytic activity toward primary-to-tertiary MTs (Fig. 2d).

To activate aromatic acids into their respective acyl-CoAs, we constructed the plasmids harboring the genes coding for an individual AAT with an ATP-dependent fatty/aromatic acid-CoA ligase (ACSL) from Thauera terpenica (TtLACSL)35, Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1 (PaLACSL)36, or ATP-dependent benzoate-CoA ligase from Hypericum (HzBCL)37. A preliminary experiment revealed that only TtLACSL exhibited benzoate-CoA activation activity when benzoate and geraniol were co-fed to the strains co-expressing individual ACSL or BCL with FaAAT. We then constructed strains with plasmids co-expressing TtLACSL with various AATs for further evaluation. In addition to FvAAT, FaAAT, LiAAT4, and ScAAT1, we validated three benzyl alcohol O-benzoyltransferases (BABTs) to assess their activities on aromatic acid-derived MTE formation. PhBABT was previously reported to esterify aromatic acid-derived acyl-CoAs with linalool and geraniol38. Identified via BLAST with ≥70% sequence identity to PhBABT in NCBI protein database, we included two additional BABTs (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Fig. 2). The evaluation indicated that FvAAT, FaAAT, and PmBABT produced the corresponding benzoate MTEs (Fig. 2d, Supplementary Figs. 4-25). FvAAT and FaAAT exhibited a wide range of substrate specificity for various MTs for benzoyl-CoA-derived MTEs, which are widely used in the flavor, fragrance, and cosmetic industries, where they contribute sweet, floral, and fruity notes39. PmBABT showed better catalytic activity for the accessed MTs and could exclusively generate benzoate MTEs (e.g., lavandulyl benzoate, geranyl benzoate, neryl benzoate, and perillyl benzoate, Fig. 2d, Supplementary Figs. 7, 9, 11, and 13). Building on these findings, we profiled the capacity of FvAAT and FaAAT to form phenylacetyl-CoA- and phenylpropionyl-CoA-derived MTEs. The identification shows that FaAAT possesses broad catalytic activities for esterifying aromatic acid-derived acyl-CoA with multiple MTs (Fig. 2d, Supplementary Figs. 4-25).

Biosynthesis of monoterpenoate and monoterpenyl monoterpenoate ester

Primary MTs, in plant or microbe, would undergo oxidation to form corresponding MTas, typically mediated by two sequential steps conduct using alcohol dehydrogenases40, 41. We hypothesized that the activation of MTa with HS-CoA by TtLACSL would possibly form monoterpenoyl-CoA, which can be subsequently esterified with SCFAlcs into MTaE (Fig. 3a). This design enables the expansion of microbial ME diversity by leveraging AAT promiscuity towards underexplored dual-substrate reactions. We evaluated the activities of FvAAT, FaAAT, LiAAT4, ScAAT1, ScEEB1, ScEHT1-1, ScEHT1-2, PmBABT, MsBABT, and PhBABT, to form MTaTE (Fig. 3b, the last three were not shown in the figure as no product was detected). By pairing two MTas with three SCFAlcs for the bioconversion, the analysis of the formed compounds in the organic phase using GC-MS showed that (S)-(-)-perillic acid was successfully activated with HS-CoA by TtLACSL and esterified by FaAAT, LiAAT4, and ScEHT1-2 into three respective MTaEs, namely ethyl (S)-(-)-perillate, propyl (S)-(-)-perillate, and butyl (S)-(-)-perillate (Fig. 3b-d). The fragmentation of these MTaEs during ionization would generate a base peak of (S)-(-)-perillic acid with an m/z = 121 (Supplementary Table 4), and characterization of these bioconversion-produced MTaEs was verified by mass spectrometry using the NMR-confirmed, chemically synthesized standards as references (Supplementary Figs. 26-28). As such, incorporating the MTaEs biosynthesized here into the ME family demonstrates the capacity to harness the promiscuity of plant-derived AATs for diversifying natural and non-natural ME biosynthesis.

The conceptual visualization of the dual-substrate ME biosynthesis inspired us to explore the biosynthesis of the third type of MEs (Fig. 1). Theoretically, monoterpenoyl-CoA activated from MTa and HS-CoA could undergo esterification by AATs using either structurally homo- or hetero-type MTs as alcohol donors, resulting in the formation of MtMtaEs (Fig. 3e). Although MtMtaE consists of four isoprene units and shares the same carbon count (C20) with canonical diterpenes, they are structurally distinct as they are not synthesized via the geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate pathway. We paired and co-fed 11 MTs with two MTas into the medium to explore the possibility of MtMtaE formation by FvAAT, FaAAT, LiAAT4, ScAAT1, ScEHT1-2, PmBABET, MsBABT, and PhBABT (Fig. 3f, the last three were not shown in the figure as no product was detected). The analysis of the compounds formed in the organic phase using GC-MS revealed that both geranic acid and (S)-(-)-perillic acid could be activated by TtLACSL to their CoA molecules, which were esterified by FaAAT into four respective MtMtaEs (Fig. 3g-i). The base peaks of geranic acid and (S)-(-)-perillic acid would be m/z =69 and 121, respectively (Supplementary Table 4). The characterization of these bioconversion-produced MtMtaEs was verified by mass spectrometry with the NMR-confirmed, chemically synthesized standards as references (Supplementary Figs. 29-31). MtMtaEs represent a unique class of monoterpene dimers with the molecular formula C20H30O2, previously detected in atmospheric secondary organic aerosols42, yet their biosynthetic origins in living organisms remain largely unexplored. The dual-substrate microbial platform accelerates the discovery and characterization of MtMtaEs, offering a viable method for biosynthesizing monoterpene dimeric esters. Importantly, the conversion of volatile and membrane-permeable monoterpenes into bulkier MtMtaEs alters their physicochemical properties, reducing volatility while favoring sequestration in subcellular storage compartments such as lipid droplets or peroxisomes. Such compartmentalization not only possibly alleviates product toxicity but also establishes a stable reservoir that supports more efficient and sustainable monoterpene biosynthesis.

Reprogramming AAT selectivity via single-residue mutagenesis and dual-substrate ratio

We performed molecular docking of the AlphaFold2-predicted FaAAT, LiAAT4, FvAAT, and PmBABT in complex with acyl-CoAs, revealing distinct differences in active-site organization that underlie their distinct substrate preferences (Supplementary Fig. 32). Although these AATs share a conserved acyl-CoA binding framework coordinated by key catalytic residues (e.g., His and Asp), the composition and geometry of the acyl-binding pocket vary substantially. FaAAT and FvAAT, which preferentially accept short-chain acyl donors, possess relatively narrow and hydrophobic acyl pockets shaped by residues such as Ala/Val and Phe/Leu, forming a compact environment around acetyl-CoA (Supplementary Fig. 32a-b). In contrast, LiAAT4 exhibits a more restricted cavity due to substitution by bulkier residues (e.g., Tyr), whereas PmBABT displays a distinct adaptation for aromatic substrates, with benzoyl-CoA stabilized by expanded hydrophobic contacts and additional polar interactions (Supplementary Fig. 32c-d). Consistent with these pocket-level differences, substrate tunnel architectures across these AATs differ in length, bottleneck radius, and residue composition (Supplementary Fig. 33). FaAAT and FvAAT feature extended tunnels that can accommodate elongated aliphatic substrates, whereas PmBABT exhibits shorter and more constrained pathways. These global tunnel features rationalize broad differences in substrate scope among AATs; however, they primarily govern substrate accessibility rather than fine discrimination between structurally similar acyl donors. In particular, the precise selectivity of FaAAT toward acetyl- versus butyryl-CoA cannot be explained by tunnel geometry alone, implicating localized interactions and dynamic effects near the catalytic center.

Accordingly, we focused on FaAAT to further investigate how ligand-binding residues govern acetyl-CoA versus butyryl-CoA selectivity using geraniol as a fixed alcohol donor. Molecular docking using the AlphaFold2-predicted FaAAT suggested that acyl-CoA binds within a shared pocket adjacent to the catalytic residue His157, with 303Phe, 162Gly, 250His, 378Ser, and 380Trp located in close proximity to the acyl-CoA moiety (Supplementary Fig. 34). Among them, 303Phe was proposed as a key residue proximal to 157His that influences the relative binding geometry of C2 and C4 acyl-CoAs to geraniol (Fig. 4a-b, Supplementary Fig. 34a). To test this hypothesis, structure-guided NDT codon-based saturation mutagenesis (N = A/C/G/T, D = A/G/T, T = thymine) was performed. Several variants exhibited selectively enhanced on butyryl-CoA over acetyl-CoA (Supplementary Fig. 34b-f). Replacement of 303Phe with small side-chain residues (e.g., Gly, Ser, and Asn) significantly reduced GA formation without causing a substantial decrease in geranyl butyrate (GB) titer. Additional substitutions at G162, H250, S378, and W380 on F303GFaAAT did not yield further improvements in selectivity or product titer (Supplementary Fig. 35), indicating that, for short-chain acyl-CoA discrimination in FaAAT, double-site tunnel reshaping is less effective than localized residue engineering near the catalytic center, likely as excessive tunnel perturbation compromises productive acyl-CoA positioning.

Phylogenetic analysis revealed substantial diversity among plant-derived AATs; however, a conserved aromatic or bulky aliphatic residue (Tyr, Phe, or Ile) is frequently observed at position 303 (Fig. 4c, Supplementary Fig. 36). Furthermore, mutagenesis at position 303 in FaAAT resulted in substrate-dependent changes in the production profiles of MTaEs and MtMtaEs (Supplementary Fig. 37), indicating that this residue influences acyl-donor preference beyond the geraniol-based system.

Representative poses of acetyl-CoA-geraniol and butyryl-CoA-geraniol complexes generated from the AlphaFold2-predicted F303GFaAAT revealed altered substrate orientations and contact patterns in the vicinity of the active site after mutation (Fig. 4d-e). However, because molecular docking provides only static and non-unique binding hypotheses, we then examined mutation-induced effects using pre-reaction state (PRS) molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. These analyses revealed that the F303G mutation does not uniformly shorten substrate contact distances but instead redistributes dynamic interaction patterns within the acyl-CoA thioester environment, particularly involving 284Asn and 378Ser, in a substrate-dependent manner (Supplementary Fig. 38). Moreover, comparative perturbation response scanning molecular dynamics (PRS-MD) analyses revealed that homologous mutations in closely related FaAAT2 can modulate distinct reaction coordinates. In FaAAT, the F303G mutation primarily reshapes thioester torsional conformations, whereas in FaAAT2 with an isoleucine at the corresponding position, the analogous I303G mutation in FaAAT2 alters the Bürgi-Dunitz attack geometry. This divergence indicates that mutation-induced selectivity arises from enzyme-specific reorganization of reactive conformational ensembles rather than static distance changes alone (Supplementary Fig. 39).

The intracellular availability of acyl-CoA and MT affects the apparent specificity of dual-substrate esterification catalyzed by AATs, which can be modulated by varying the molar ratio of the substrates. To confirm this, we profiled the formations of GB and GA at varying dual-substrate molar ratios, both wtFaAAT and F303GFaAAT exhibited high exponential curve fitting confidence for GA and GB formation (R2>0.99, Fig. 4f, Supplementary Data 3, No. 31-34). The selectivity for GLB formation was improved at all tested dual-substrate molar ratios (Fig. 4g). The strain harboring F303GFaAAT achieved a GB selectivity of 98.95% under a 4:1 butyrate-to-geraniol molar ratio, representing a 3.12-fold (p < 0.001) increase relative to wtFaAAT under a 1:4 ratio; even under 1:4 butyrate-to-geraniol molar ratio, F303GFaAAT still exhibited a 2.21-fold improvement in GB selectivity compared with wtFaAAT (p < 0.001; Fig. 4g). Consistent with this trend, the other two beneficial substitutions at position 303 of FaAAT also showed improved GB selectivity under higher butyrate-to-geraniol ratios (Supplementary Fig. 34g-i).

To elucidate the enzymatic basis underlying these mutation-enhanced selectivity effects, we next characterized the intrinsic catalytic properties of wtFaAAT and F303GFaAAT in vitro. The F303G mutation in FaAAT resulted in no detectable product in the acetyl-CoA/geraniol reaction, indicating a loss of enzyme catalytic activity toward acetyl-CoA upon introduction of the F303G mutation under the tested conditions in vitro (Fig. 4h, Supplementary Figs. 40-41). In contrast, for the butyryl-CoA/geraniol reaction, quantitative kinetic analysis was feasible. The Km value showed no significant change upon mutation (1.04-fold difference relative to the wild type, p = 0.66), indicating that substrate binding affinity for butyryl-CoA was largely preserved. However, the catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) was significantly reduced to 0.35-fold of wtFaAAT (p < 0.001) (Fig. 4h, Supplementary Fig. 40). These kinetics are consistent with mutation-induced destabilization of catalytically productive acetyl-CoA conformations, arising from altered local hydrogen-bonding networks involving 284Asn and 378Ser, while largely preserving butyryl-CoA binding (Supplementary Fig. 42).

Despite the favorable shift in acyl-donor preference conferred by the F303G mutation in FaAAT, the overall catalytic performance of FaAAT remained constrained under cellular conditions, prompting us to examine whether enzyme solubility represents an additional limiting factor. We observed poor soluble expression of both wtFaAAT and F303GFaAAT (Supplementary Fig. 40a), which likely caused the reduced catalytic activity for GB formation (Fig. 4f and 4i). Phylogenetic analysis and pairwise sequence alignment revealed that FaAAT2, identified from the NCBI protein database (Supplementary Fig. 40b-c), contains an Ile at position 303 and differs from FaAAT by five amino acid residues (Supplementary Fig. 36), showing improved solubility compared with FaAAT (Supplementary Fig. 40d). Profiling GB and GA production by the strains expressing wtFaAAT2 and I303GFaAAT2 varying molar ratios of butyrate-to-geraniol generated high-confidence exponential curve fitting (Supplementary Fig. 43, R²>0.98, Supplementary Data 3, No. 39-42) and a GB titer (Fig. 4i) approaching the theoretical yield (1.45 g/L, Supplementary Fig. 44). The GB selectivity achieved by the strain harboring I303GFaAAT2 (97.62%) was slightly lower than that of F303GFaAAT under a 4:1 molar ratio of butyrate-to-geraniol, but still represented a 4.22-fold increase compared to wtFaAAT2 under 1:4 molar ratio of butyrate-to-geraniol (p < 0.001) (Fig. 4j). The enhanced GB selectivity observed with I303GFaAAT2 was consistent with altered catalytic behavior, as confirmed by steady-state kinetic assays (Fig. 4k, Supplementary Fig. 40e-f), which suggests that, in FaAAT2, the apparent acyl-CoA selectivity is governed by a combined contribution of catalytic turnover, enzyme solubility, and global active-site interaction networks (Supplementary Fig. 45), rather than being solely dictated by local acyl-CoA binding energetics.

To place these enzyme determinants within a unified catalytic framework, we next examined the intrinsic reaction mechanism shared by AAT and its variants. The kinetic data are consistent with a sequential bi-bi mechanism for AAT and its variants under the tested conditions, in which geraniol and acyl-CoA form a catalytically competent ternary complex (Fig. 4I, Supplementary Fig. 46-47). To quantitatively address the catalytic mechanism, we have performed ab initio QM calculations on an enzyme model that encompasses the core reaction center (157His in FaAAT, geraniol, and CoA thioester, Supplementary Fig. 48). This model confirms the proposed mechanism: 157His facilitates geraniol deprotonation followed by nucleophilic attack on the thioester carbonyl, with a rate-determining barrier of 17.6 kcal/mol (ΔHǂ). Notably, the subsequent proton transfer from the imidazolium to thiolate is essentially barrierless, and the overall reaction is slightly exergonic (ΔG = -3.1 kcal/mol). The computed energy profile aligns well with the mechanistic scheme in Fig. 4I, suggesting the critical role of pre-organized active-site architecture in transition-state stabilization. Building on this mechanistic understanding, to validate the combined strategy of single-residue engineering and dual-substrate ratio control for precision ester biosynthesis, we characterized more substrate pairings: butyryl-CoA with nerol, butanol, and benzyl alcohol; geraniol with propionyl-CoA and benzoyl-CoA; and benzoyl-CoA with benzoyl-CoA. Exponential fittings of the product titers on the selected dual-substrate molar ratio showed high confidence (average R²>0.98 across all dual-substrate pairings (Supplementary Data 3, No. 1-30, 47-72). Modulating molar ratios of acyl-CoA-to-alcohol from 4:1 to 1:4 with varied wtAAT and its mutants significantly enhanced selectivity by 3.71-fold (neryl butyrate, p < 0.001), 1.94-fold (butyl butyrate, p < 0.001), 3.19-fold (benzyl butyrate, p < 0.001), 2.10-fold (geranyl propionate, p < 0.001), 60.13-fold (geranyl benzoate, p < 0.001), and 1.37-fold (benzyl benzoate, p < 0.001) (Supplementary Figs. 49-54), outperforming the reported AATs under comparable conditions (Supplementary Fig. 44). These results support that dual-substrate molar ratio modulation adjusts the apparent AAT selectivity, while critical residue engineering alters the AAT’s intrinsic specificity, both of which aided precision ester biosynthesis.

Coculture to de novo monoterpenoate ester biosynthesis

Connecting isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) plus dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP) or only two DMAPPs generates various prenyl diphosphate (PDSP) by PDP synthase (PDPS). Subsequent releasing diphosphate from PDP by MT synthase (MTS) would form corresponding MTs (Supplementary Fig. 55a)24. To establish de novo MT biosynthetic route from glycerol in E. coli, six representative MTs were selected—linalool, geraniol, α-terpineol, borneol, nerol, and lavandulol—covering primary, secondary, and tertiary MTs. The entire biosynthetic pathway was modularly assembled with four units: an upstream mevalonate (MVA) module, a downstream MVA module, a PDPS module, and an MTS module. Each module operon-related gene was placed under the control of two inducible promoters, enabling fine-tuned flux regulation (Supplementary Fig. 56-61). Systematic metabolic engineering revealed several key strategies to enhance MT production: increasing acetyl-CoA availability through the ethanol utilization pathway (EUP)43, 44, optimizing gene expression across modules to balance pathway flux, and reducing by-product formation via targeted gene deletions (Supplementary Fig. 55b-g, Supplementary Figs. 56-61). For GPP-derived MTs, changing MTSs in the downstream biosynthetic pathway resulted in evident differences in product titers (Supplementary Fig. 55b-e). Under optimized strain and induction conditions, the titers of linalool, geraniol, α-terpineol, borneol, and nerol reached 3.33 g/L, 1.18 g/L, 198.98 mg/L, 3.84 mg/L, and 224.42 mg/L, respectively. The titer of linalool achieved was 16.74-fold higher (p < 0.001) than that of α-terpineol. This disparity is attributable to differences among MTSs in both catalytic efficiency toward GPP and effective expression levels24, resulting in varied production titers of MTs. Besides, protein engineering of MTS to enhance their activities was therefore critical for improving MT biosynthesis. In lavandulol biosynthesis, we screened a panel of E. coli endogenous phosphatases and identified EcRdgB as the most active enzyme toward lavandulyl pyrophosphate. We further performed structure-guided multiple-round single-site mutagenesis to enhance its catalytic efficiency, obtaining the engineered variant F118D-H182CEcRdgB, which significantly improved the hydrolysis of lavandulyl pyrophosphate and consequently increased the lavandulol titer by 7.64-fold (p < 0.001) (Supplementary Fig. 61).

Inspired by the modularity of acyl-CoA and MT biosynthetic pathways in nature, we constructed a MT-producing strain and an ester-producing strain for coculture engineering (Supplementary Fig. 62a). This strategy simplifies the genetic manipulation cycle and alleviates metabolic competition for shared precursors such as acetyl-CoA45. By combining the above MT-producing strains with an esterification module containing AATs with defined substrate specificity, we produced natural linalyl acetate (LA) and GB via microbial biosynthesis. LA and GB have high industrial relevance: LA is the dominant high-value fragrance component in lavender essential oil and is widely used in perfumery, while GB is a commercially important fruity/floral flavor compound used in food, beverage, and fragrance formulations27, 46. Besides, their biosynthetic precursors—linalool and geraniol—are among the monoterpene alcohols with the higher achievable microbial titers in this study and other extensive studies, enabling a representative demonstration of MTEs biosynthesis. For acetate MTE biosynthesis using a single strain, introducing an additional plasmid overexpressing LiAAT4 with an inducible promoter into the linalool-producing strain would be achieved. However, even under optimized induction conditions, the highest titer of LA reached 0.058 g/L by the single-strain mode (Fig. 5a-b, Supplementary Fig. 63). We cocultured the linalool-producing strain with the ester-producing strain containing LiAAT4 (Fig. 5c) and optimized the critical parameters. Optimization of inoculation ratio at the induction stage, coupled with EUP module integration into the ester-producing strain, substantially enhanced LA production (Supplementary Fig. 63), achieving a titer of 3.22 g/L, representing a 55.2-fold improvement over monoculture systems (p < 0.001) (Fig. 5b). Next, to construct a single-strain system for GB production, we transformed the third plasmid with the genes coding the enzymes of butyryl-CoA biosynthetic pathway47 and wtFaAAT into the geraniol-producing strain (Fig. 5d, Supplementary Fig. 64). However, this three-plasmid-containing strain did not give a detectable titer of GB after optimizing the induction conditions for pathway balancing (Fig. 5e). We subsequently cocultured a geraniol-producing strain and a strain with butyryl-CoA biosynthetic pathway and wtFaAAT, which produced 0.077 g/L of GB (Fig. 5e-f). Because wtFaAAT provided a consistent baseline for optimizing coculture conditions, we subsequently replaced it with F303GFaAAT and I303GFaAAT2 in the ester-producing strain, which increased the GB titer to 0.32 g/L with a selectivity of 97.81% (Fig. 5e, Supplementary Fig. 64). We further expanded the product profile to biosynthesize acetate and butyrate MTEPs from glycerol using coculture strategy, and achieved the titers of lavandulyl acetate, neryl acetate, bornyl acetate, lavandulyl butyrate, and neryl butyrate to 94.49, 197.12, 2.40, 8.72, and 65.72 mg/L (Fig. 5g-k, Supplementary Fig. 62b-f).

To scale up the coculture process for ME biosynthesis, we ran fed-batch fermentation in a 1-liter bioreactor. A titer of 11.50 g/L LA was obtained, with 0.11 g/L linalool residing after 96h fermentation (Fig. 5l). Chiral column analysis of the fermenter samples confirmed the stereoselective biosynthesis of R-(–)-LA in enantiopure form, in contrast to chemically synthesized racemic LA (RS-mixture, Supplementary Fig. 62g). The GB-producing coculture reached a titer of 3.16 g/L, with 0.033 g/L GA and 0.046 g/L geraniol accumulated after 83 h, corresponding to a GB selectivity of 98.97% (Fig. 5m). Importantly, GB was obtained as an isomerically pure compound, whereas chemically synthesized standards consisted of mixed isomers including neryl butyrate (Supplementary Fig. 62h). In both cases, the target esters were captured in situ by an overlaying organic phase, which enabled efficient product partitioning from the aqueous broth and visual accumulation of ester-rich layers for further downstream purification (Fig. 5n and 5o). These results highlight the scalability, specificity, and stereochemical fidelity of the coculture strategy for de novo biosynthesis of MEs.
paper_content.methods:
Strains, chemicals, and culture media

The primers and genes used in this study were synthesized at Sangon Biotech Shanghai Co., Ltd., China and Jiutian Gene Technology (Tianjin) Co., Ltd, China. The sequence information of primers and genes are listed in Supplementary Data 4 and Supplementary Data 5. E. coli DH5α (TSC-C01-100, Beijing Tsingke Biotechnology Co., Ltd, China) was used for general cloning purposes. E. coli MG1655(DE3) ∆endA ∆recA (https://www.addgene.org/37854/) was used for fermentation. E. coli BL21(DE3) (TSC-E01, Beijing Tsingke Biotechnology Co., Ltd, China) was used for protein purification. All the chemicals used in this study are listed in Supplementary Data 6. For genome editing of E. coli MG1655(DE3) ΔendA ΔrecA, a two-plasmid CRISSPR-Cas9 system was used56, and the pTarget plasmids employed are detailed in Supplementary Data 7 and 8. Colony PCR was used to evaluate the correctness of the genes deleted at the selected locus. Fermentation process for ME formation identification was carried out in M2 medium (pH 7.0), consisting of 10 g/L glycerol, 26.6 g/L K2HPO4, 8 g/L (NH4)2HPO4, 12 g/L tryptone (LP0042B, Oxoid, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., USA), 24 g/L yeast extract (LP0021B, Oxoid, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., USA), and appropriate antibiotics.

Plasmid construction and transformation

The construction of the plasmids in this study was based on the GT DNA assembly standard57 when designing overlapping sequences. The assembly of all the PCR-obtained DNA fragments was done using the homologous recombination enzyme (2 × ClonExpress Mix, KAO-201, Toro Bioscience, China) and carried out with an equimolar amount of each DNA fragment in a PCR instrument at 50 °C for 15~30 mins. The standard heat-shock protocol was used to transform the assembled mixture into E. coli DH5α. The culture plate was incubated overnight at 37 °C until the colonies reached an appropriate size, after which they were harvested for subsequent colony PCR verification. The colonies containing the corrected plasmid assembly were inoculated into 5 mL LB medium and used to extract the plasmids for Sanger sequencing. All the plasmids constructed are listed in Supplementary Data 7 and 8. The standard electroporation protocol transformed the sequencing-confirmed plasmid into E. coli MG1655(DE3) ∆endA ∆recA or other derivative strains. All the strains constructed and used in this study are listed in Supplementary Data 9.

Bioconversion of paired MT with acid into ME

The expression plasmids carrying individual AAT (Supplementary Data 7 and 8) were transformed into E. coli MG1655(DE3) ∆endA ∆recA. A single colony of the resulting strain was inoculated into 1 mL LB medium (ampicillin 50 μg/mL) and incubated overnight as the seed culture. Next, 2% (v/v) of seed culture was inoculated into 2 mL M2 medium with 50 μg/mL ampicillin into 2 mL of culture medium in a 15 mL high-borosilicate glass test tube (15 × 150 mm, Product No. 120307005, Changde Beckman Biotechnology Co., Ltd, China). Upon reaching OD600 of 1.0, isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG, 0.1 mM), the pairing substrates of acid and alcohol were added. For MTE biosynthesis, 20 μL of acid substrate (100 g/L aqueous stocks) was added at a final concentration of ~1 g/L. MTs dissolved in dodecane or hexadecane (6.67 g/L) were added into the culture with 300 μL (15% v/v) to a final concentration of 1 g/L. For MTaE biosynthesis, geranic acid or (S)-(-)-perillic acid (500 g/L in dimethyl sulfoxide, DMSO) was added with 4 μL to a final concentration of ~1 g/L, followed by adding 20 μL of alcohol substrate (ethanol, propanol, butanol) in ultrapure water (100 g/L) into the culture. Subsequently, 300 μL of dodecane overlay was supplemented for in situ product extraction during fermentation. For MtMtaE biosynthesis, MTa and MT were paired and supplemented at the same final concentration as specified above. The cultures were incubated at 30 °C, 250 rpm for 30 h. After fermentation, the upper organic phase was collected after centrifugation at 16,000 g for 5 min, and 10 μL of the upper phase was mixed with 190 μL ethyl acetate for GC-MS analysis.

Bioconversion of paired substrates into other esters

To biosynthesize butyl butyrate, benzyl benzoate, and benzyl butyrate, the expression plasmids carrying individual AAT (Supplementary Data 7 and 8) were transformed into E. coli MG1655(DE3) ∆endA ∆recA. The culture processes are as described in “Bioconversion of paired MT with acid into ME”). The concentration of butanol or benzyl alcohol was 1 g/L (100 g/L aqueous stock), and butyrate or benzoate was added into the culture with a molar ratio of acid-to-alcohol of 2:1 for screening strains containing mutants of AAT. For the dual-substrate molar ratio test, the alcohol was still fixed at 1 g/L, and the acid substrate was added in the ratios of 4:1, 2:1, 1:1, 1:2, and 1:4. For benzyl benzoate, the concentration of benzyl alcohol was reduced to 0.3 g/L to avoid cellular toxicity when evaluating the dual-substrate molar ratio.

Metabolite analysis

GC-MS analysis: A 2 μL aliquot of the above-obtained mixtures of organic solvents with ethyl acetate was used for GC-MS analysis. GC-MS was performed using a system equipped with HP-5MS Capillary Column (30 m × 0.25 mm × 0.25 μm, Agilent Technologies, CA, USA) in a split ratio 1:10. The oven temperature program was as follows: initial hold at 50 °C for 1 min, ramp to 100 °C at 5 °C/min (5 min hold), then to 200 °C at 5 °C/min (5 min hold), followed by a 5 °C/min ramp to 300 °C (5 min hold). The MS source and quadrupole were maintained at 230 °C and 150 °C, respectively, with a scan range of 40-500 m/z. When exporting the extracted ion chromatograms (EIC) based on the information provided in Supplementary Table 3-4 and Supplementary Data 2, fixed offsets were applied to the Y-axis to distinguish the chromatographic traces of different samples for clearer visualization, and the X-axis range was constrained to focus on the regions of interest. It should be noted that these adjustments were made solely to optimize the graphical presentation, and all original raw data remain complete and unaltered, which are fully provided in Supplementary Data 10. GC-MS spectra exported from the instrument software (Agilent MassHunter Workstation Software, Version B.07.00). For each spectrum, the exported table (CSV format, Supplementary Data 11) was parsed by skipping the first two metadata/header lines and extracting the m/z and ion-count columns. Peak intensities were normalized to relative intensity (%) by setting the base peak to 100 (intensity/max intensity × 100). The normalized spectra were then rendered as mass spectra with uniform peak-line width, and the 15 most intense ions were annotated by their m/z values.

GC analysis: GC analysis was conducted using a GC9720Plus (Zhejiang Fuli Analytical Instruments Co., Ltd, China) or Agilent 8860 (Agilent Technologies, CA, USA) equipped with an HP-5MS capillary column (30 m × 0.25 mm × 0.25 μm, Agilent Technologies, CA, USA) or Chiral GC capillary column, Rt-βDEXse (30 m × 0.32 mm × 0.25 μm, Restek Corporation, PA, USA). Post-fermentation, 20 μL of the organic phase sample was mixed with 80 μL of ethyl acetate for GC analysis. A 2 μL aliquot of the mixture of organic solvents with ethyl acetate was injected into the GC for analysis. For the HP-5MS capillary column, the oven temperature program was initiated with an isothermal hold at 50 °C for 2 min, followed by a controlled temperature ramp at a rate of 15 °C/min up to 250 °C, where it was maintained for an additional 7 min to ensure optimal separation. For the Chiral GC capillary column, the oven temperature was programmed as follows: held at 50 °C for 1 min, increased to 100 °C at a rate of 10 °C/min and held for 1 min, then raised to 120 °C at a rate of 0.5 °C/min and held for 1 min, and finally increased to 230 °C at a rate of 20 °C/min and held for 2 min.

HPLC analysis: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analysis was conducted using an LC-20A system (Shimadzu, Japan) equipped with an Aminex HPX-87H Column (300 × 7.8 mm, Bio-Rad Laboratories, Inc., USA). To quantify glycerol, ethanol, and other fermentation metabolites, 1 mL of cell culture supernatant was collected from centrifuging (16,000 g, 5 min) at each sampling time point and filtered. A 10 μL of the obtained samples was injected for analysis. The separation was performed under isocratic conditions with a mobile phase of 5 mM H2SO4 aqueous solution at a flow rate of 0.7 mL/min. The column temperature was maintained at 40 °C, and analytes were detected using a refractive index detector. Commercial standards of glycerol and acetate were employed to establish calibration curves for accurate concentration determination.

Sequence alignment and phylogenetic tree analysis of AATs

Protein sequences of AATs (Supplementary Data 5) were aligned using ClustalW with default gap penalties (gap opening: 10.0; extension: 0.10 for pairwise and 0.20 for multiple alignments). Divergent sequences were delayed using a 30% cutoff. Phylogenetic analysis was conducted using MEGA software employing the Maximum Likelihood method58. The Jones-Taylor-Thornton model was selected for amino acid substitution59, with uniform rates among sites and inclusion of all sites in the analysis. The initial tree was automatically generated using the BioNJ method. The ML heuristic method applied was Nearest-Neighbor Interchange, and the analysis was run using four computational threads. The resulting aligned FASTA file containing 14 AATs was submitted to the ESPript 3.0 server (https://espript.ibcp.fr/ESPript/ESPript/) for structure-informed alignment annotation60. A corresponding PDB file of FvAAT was uploaded to map secondary structure elements onto the alignment. Besides, to create pairwise alignment with each two AAT protein sequences, the FASTA file containing 14 AATs (Supplementary Data 5) was used for sequence similarity calculation in the Biopython pairwise2 module with the globalxx scoring scheme in Python 3.1261. The similarity score between each pair of protein sequences was normalized by the length of the shorter sequence and expressed as a percentage. A similarity matrix was constructed and visualized as a heatmap using the Seaborn and Matplotlib libraries in Python 3.12.

Structure modeling

Protein structural models of AATs and their mutants were generated using AlphaFold62 (https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/) or SWISS-MODEL63 (https://swissmodel.expasy.org/), depending on sequence availability and prior structural annotation. For AAT structures not available in the AlphaFold database, homology models were constructed using the SWISS-MODEL server. Protein sequences were submitted to the SWISS-MODEL workspace, and the top-ranked template based on sequence identity and coverage was selected for model generation. All resulting models were confirmed as monomers unless otherwise indicated. Template entries and sequence identity (%) between query proteins and their corresponding structural templates are summarized in Supplementary Table 5. The modeled structures were used for active site residue mapping, enzyme-ligand docking, and tunnel analysis.

Molecular docking

Molecular docking of AATs with selected ligands was performed using AutoDock Vina v1.1.264. Three-dimensional ligand structures were retrieved from the PubChem database (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov) and converted to PDB format using Open Babel65. Ligand and protein preparation, including the addition of Gasteiger charges and polar hydrogen atoms, was conducted using AutoDock Tools v1.5.666. Docking was carried out between each AAT model and its corresponding ligand, with docking grids centered around the putative active sites of dual substrates based on the results of tunnel analysis. All docking parameters, including grid box size, center coordinates, and exhaustiveness values are available via Zenodo67.

AAT substrate tunnel analysis

Dual-substrate access tunnels of AATs were analyzed using the CAVER 3.0.3 PyMOL plugin (integrated in PyMOL 3.1.0, Schrödinger)68, 69. The analysis was performed on the representative AAT PDB structures. The starting point for tunnel calculation was defined as the N3 atom of the catalytically relevant histidine in the active site. The following parameters were used for tunnel detection: probe radius of 0.9 Å, shell radius of 3.0 Å, and shell depth of 4.0 Å. For tunnel clustering and prioritization, default settings were applied. All tunnels were visually inspected and rendered using PyMOL. Key surrounding residues were annotated for each identified tunnel, and comparative analysis was performed across different mutants to assess changes in tunnel geometry and accessibility. The tunnel analysis pse files are available via Zenodo67.

Synthesis of chemical standards

The chemical standards of MTaE and MtMtaE were synthesized as follows70: (1) to synthesize ethyl, propyl, and butyl (S)-(-)-perillate, a mixture of perillic acid (1.52 g) and potassium carbonate (1.93 g) was dissolved in 20 mL of dimethylformamide (DMF). Under stirring at room temperature, a solution of iodoethane/iodopropane/iodobutane (1.87/2.04/2.21 g) in DMF was added dropwise. After completion, the reaction mixture was heated to 40 °C and stirred for 5 h. The mixture was then quenched with saturated brine (10 mL), and the aqueous layer was extracted with ethyl acetate. The combined organic phases were washed with saturated brine, dried over anhydrous sodium sulfate, concentrated, and purified by column chromatography to afford the target compounds as colorless liquids. (2) to synthesize perillyl generate, the reaction was carried out under a nitrogen atmosphere. Iodine (3.81 g) was dissolved in 150 mL of dry dichloroethane at room temperature (25 °C), followed by sequential addition of PPh3 (3.94g), imidazole (2.25 g), and geranic acid (1.85 g). The mixture was stirred for 15 min before adding Gd(OTf)3 (0.06 g) and heating to 45~50 °C for 30 min. Subsequently, perillyl alcohol (1.52 g) was added, and the reaction temperature was maintained for 2~3 h until completion was confirmed by thin-layer chromatography (petroleum ether:ethyl acetate=20:1, v/v). The workup involved quenching with 1 M sodium bicarbonate solution (100 mL) with 10 min of stirring. After phase separation, the aqueous layer was further extracted with dichloroethane (50 mL). The combined organic phases were washed with saturated brine, dried over anhydrous sodium sulfate, concentrated, and purified by column chromatography to afford the target compounds as oily liquid. (3) to synthesize geranyl generate and geranyl (S)-(-)-perillate, under a nitrogen atmosphere at room temperature (25 °C), iodine (3.81 g) was dissolved in 150 mL of anhydrous dichloroethane, followed by the addition of PPh3 (3.94 g), imidazole (2.25 g), and geranic acid (1.85 g)/(S)-(-)-perillic acid (1.83 g). The mixture was stirred for an additional 15 min. Then Gd(OTf)3 (0.06 g) was introduced, and the temperature was raised to 45~50 °C with continuous stirring for 30 min. Geraniol (1.54 g) was added, and the reaction was maintained for 2~3 h until completion, as monitored by thin-layer chromatography (petroleum ether: ethyl acetate=20:1, v/v). The reaction mixture was quenched with 1M sodium bicarbonate solution (100 mL) and stirred for 10 min. After phase separation, the aqueous layer was further extracted with dichloroethane (50 mL). The combined organic phases were washed with saturated brine, dried over anhydrous sodium sulfate, concentrated, and purified by column chromatography to afford the target compounds as oily liquid. All the structures of the products were confirmed by ¹H NMR (Bruker 400 MHz, CDCl3). The spectra were processed and analyzed using MestReNova 14.0.

Construction of NDT-based mutagenesis library and screening

Based on the analysis of molecular docking of AATs with ligands, the critical residues were identified for creating the NDT-based saturation or site-directed mutagenesis library. In brief, the primers containing NDT degenerate codons were introduced during PCR and assembled into the corresponding plasmid backbone. All primer sequences can be found in Supplementary Data 4. The plasmids carrying the mixture of mutants were then assembled, and the assembly mixture was transformed into E. coli DH5α, which were plated on LB agar with appropriate antibiotics and incubated overnight at 37 °C. Next, the colonies formed the next day were washed out 5-10 times using 5 mL LB medium until all the colonies were collected, followed by plasmid extraction to obtain the mixed mutant plasmid pool. The plasmids carrying the mixture of mutants were transformed into E. coli MG1655(DE3) ∆endA ∆recA or other derivative strains and cultured overnight at 37 °C. To assess library quality, six colonies were sequenced to confirm the presence of the desired mutations. Then, 30 colonies, approximately converging at three times of library size, were cultured to evaluate the production of MEs (the alcohol concentration is maintained at 1 g/L of final concentration, with acid employed as a co-substrate at a fixed molar ratio. The acid-to-alcohol molar ratio is set at 1:4 for screening butyl butyrate, benzyl butyrate, and geranyl propionate, and at 2:1 for all other combinations) (Details can be found in “Bioconversion of paired MT with acid into ME”). Site-directed mutagenesis was conducted by designing the primers for the other 19 mutations (Supplementary Data 4). After the plasmid assembly, the plasmid with the mutant gene was transformed into E. coli DH5α. A single colony was selected and cultured overnight in 10 mL LB medium with appropriate antibiotics at 37 °C and 250 rpm. The plasmid was then extracted for sequencing to confirm the mutation, followed by transformation into the corresponding E. coli MG1655(DE3) ∆endA ∆recA or other derivative strains. The resulting strains were then used for evaluating the production of MEs. The strains with top-performing mutants were sequenced to determine the substitution of amino acids (Details can be found in “Bioconversion of paired MT with acid into ME”).

Profiling the formations of MTEs at varied dual-substrate molar ratios

Following initial screening, the strains harboring the mixture of the NDT-based saturation AAT mutants or site-directed mutants were investigated to determine the effect of dual-substrate molar ratio on the formation of acetate MTE and target MTE. A single colony was inoculated into 1 mL of LB medium containing 50 μg/mL of ampicillin for overnight incubation at 37 °C and 250 rpm to generate the seed culture. Subsequently, 2% (v/v) of the seed culture was transferred into 2 mL of M2 medium containing 50 μg/mL ampicillin in test tubes and incubated at 37 °C with shaking at 250 rpm. Once the OD600 of the culture reached 2.0, isopropyl-β-d-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) was added to a final concentration of 0.1 mM to induce enzyme expression. The alcohol substrate was added at a final concentration of 1 g/L with 20% (v/v) of organic solvent added to each culture (5 g/L alcohol stock in dodecane or hexadecane; for the synthesis of benzyl benzoate, 1.5 g/L benzyl alcohol in dodecane). Acid substrates were prepared as 200 g/L aqueous stock and added into the cultures with varying volumes to adjust molar ratios of acid-to-alcohol at 0 (no additional acid), 1:4, 1:2, 1:1, 2:1, and 4:1 (for the combination of geraniol and propionate, the molar ratio of acid-to-alcohol was adjusted from 2:1 to 10:1). The cultures were then incubated at 30 °C with shaking at 250 rpm for 24 h. After fermentation, cells were separated by centrifugation at 16,000 g for 5 min, and 20 μL from the upper organic phase was mixed with 80 μL of ethyl acetate and subjected to GC analysis. To evaluate the selectivity of AAT or its mutants to GB formation, the percentage of GB titer to the sum of GB and GA titers was calculated.

Curve fitting of MTE formation in bioconversion

To evaluate the formation kinetics of MTEs by various AATs and their mutants, a nonlinear regression model Equation (1) was applied to experimental data obtained under varying dual-substrate molar ratios. The course of dose-response data was fitted to a three-parameter exponential model of the form:

y = a × exp(b × x) + c (1)

where y represents the product titer (g/L), and x is the independent variable of the acid-to-alcohol molar ratio. The fitting parameters a, b, and c in the exponential model represent the initial amplitude, rate of exponential change, and final asymptotic value, respectively. The fitting procedure was implemented using the curve_fit function from the scipy.optimize module in Python 3.1271. Initial parameter guesses were set as (1, -1, 1). Model parameters (a, b, c) and the coefficient of determination (R²) were calculated for each product using least-squares regression. The fitted curves were plotted alongside the corresponding experimental data points and error bars. Fitting results, including equations and R² values, were detailed in Supplementary Data 3.

Enzyme purification

E. coli BL21(DE3) cells harboring the plasmid pHisTag-AAT with T7 promoter were cultured in a 500 mL shake flask containing 200 mL of LB medium at 37 °C for the overexpression of N-terminally His6-tagged AAT. When the OD600 of the culture reached 2.0, IPTG was added to a final concentration of 0.05 mM, and incubation continued for an additional 24 h at 30 °C. After that, the cells were harvested by centrifugation at 16,000 g for 10 min and washed once with 10 mL phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.2-7.6, B548117, Sangon Biotech Shanghai Co., Ltd., China). The cell pellet was then resuspended in 10 mL of the same buffer. Cell lysis was performed using an ultrasonic homogenizer (WM-650E, Shanghai Weimi Technology Co., Ltd., China), and the lysate was clarified by centrifugation at 16,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C. The resulting supernatant was subjected to Ni2+-affinity chromatography (PrePacked Gravity Column, C600801, Sangon Biotech Shanghai Co., Ltd., China). A total of 10 mL of the supernatant was loaded onto the pre-equilibrated Ni2+ column. The elute solution was reloaded three times to ensure maximal binding of His6-tagged AAT protein. The column was washed with an equilibration buffer containing 20 mM imidazole to remove nonspecifically bound proteins. Elution was performed stepwise with the buffers containing 40 mM, 100 mM, 200 mM, and 500 mM imidazole. Eluted fractions were collected and analyzed to determine the elution efficiency and purity of the target protein. The concentration of purified AAT was quantified using the Bradford assay in 96-well plates. Briefly, 20 μL of protein sample was mixed with 180 μL of Bradford reagent (Modified Bradford Protein Assay Kit, C503041, Sangon Biotech Shanghai Co., Ltd., China) and incubated at room temperature. The sample was measured at absorbance at 595 nm using a microplate reader (Varioskan LUX, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., USA).

in vitro enzymatic activity assay and kinetic analysis

Following protein purification, the enzymatic reactions were conducted with a volume of 500 μL. The enzyme concentration was fixed at 20 mg/L in all assays. Two experimental groups were designed to determine kinetic parameters and reaction mechanism. Group A was conducted under a fixed geraniol concentration while varying acyl-CoA (acetyl-CoA or butyryl-CoA). Geraniol was dissolved in DMSO at 1.5 g/L, and 10.2 μL was added to each reaction to a final concentration of 20 mg/L. Acyl-CoA substrates were freshly prepared at 1 g/L in 1× PBS buffer (pH 7.2–7.6), and the corresponding volume was adjusted to achieve molar ratios of geraniol-to-acyl-CoA from 1:4 to 4:1. Group B was designed with fixed acyl-CoA concentration while varying geraniol. Specifically, 10 μL of 1 g/L acetyl-CoA or butyryl-CoA was added to 20 mg/L final concentration, and geraniol was added in varying volumes from 1 g/L stock to establish molar ratios ranging from 1:2 to 8:1. In both groups, the final reaction volume was adjusted to 500 μL using PBS buffer. Reactions were incubated at 30 °C and 250 rpm for 6 h. Upon completion, 500 μL of ethyl acetate was added to each reaction for extraction, followed by shaking at 800 rpm and 30 °C for 10 min. The mixture was then centrifuged at 16,000 g for 5 min. A 200 μL aliquot of the upper organic layer was collected and analyzed via GC-MS. Steady-state kinetic data were analyzed using Python 3.12. Reaction rates from triplicate assays under varying substrate concentrations were fitted to the Michaelis–Menten equation using scipy.optimize.curve_fit to obtain Vmax and Km. Double-reciprocal (Lineweaver–Burk) plots were generated using matplotlib, with reciprocal values (1/[S], 1/V) calculated via numpy and fitted by linear regression. Standard deviations were calculated and used as error bars in all plots.

Protein and ligand structure optimization under dynamic simulation

All MD simulations were conducted using Amber1372 with the amber14SB force field for proteins. The simulation system was solvated in a TIP3P water model within a cubic water box, and neutralized by the addition of sodium counterions. Energy minimization was performed using the steepest descent algorithm for 50,000 steps. The system was equilibrated through 30 ps of NVT followed by 30 ps of NPT simulations at 300 K. A 100-ns production run was subsequently carried out. Temperature coupling was maintained via velocity rescaling73, and pressure control was achieved using the Berendsen barostat74. The SHAKE algorithm was employed to constrain all covalent bonds involving hydrogen atoms, and long-range electrostatic interactions were treated using the particle mesh Ewald method75. Short-range van der Waals interactions were truncated at 12 Å. All equations of motion were integrated using the leapfrog algorithm. Ligand structures of acetyl-CoA, butyryl-CoA, and geraniol were retrieved from PubChem76, and 3D conformers were generated using RDKit's Chem.AllChem.EmbedMolecule function77 with the ETKDG algorithm78. The generated conformations were optimized with the MMFF94 force field79, and the lowest-energy conformation was selected as the input for docking.

MD simulation of docking-derived enzyme-ligand complex

Initial coordinates for MD simulations were generated from molecular docking to provide reasonable starting configurations of enzyme-ligand complexes. To avoid bias from any single docking pose, all simulations were subsequently allowed to freely relax and sample conformational space without geometric restraints, and each MD simulation was carried out for 100 ns. The General AMBER Force Field (GAFF2)80 was used to parameterize ligand molecules, and all other simulation settings were identical to those described above. MD trajectories were analyzed to characterize the dynamic behavior of active-site regions and substrate conformations. Root mean square deviation (RMSD) analysis was used solely to assess overall trajectory stability rather than as a proxy for catalytic competence. Where applicable, binding free energy estimates were obtained using the Gmx_MMPBSA tool81. Representative trajectories and raw simulation data are available via Zenodo67.

Quantum mechanical calculations

Quantum mechanical (QM) calculations were performed using Gaussian 1682. Near-attack conformations were extracted from pre-reaction state (PRS) MD ensembles and converted into Gaussian input files83. The QM cluster models consisted of truncated CoA thioester and geraniol substrates together with key active-site residues, resulting in systems of approximately 80 atoms. Each residue was truncated at the Cα atom and capped with hydrogen atoms to satisfy valence requirements. Reaction pathways were investigated using the B3LYP-D3(BJ)/6-31+G(d,p) level of theory with implicit solvation modeled by SMD (methanol). Optimized geometries and corresponding XYZ coordinates are provided, and all raw QM data are available via Zenodo67.

Modular construction of MT biosynthetic pathway in E. coli.

A two-plasmid system comprising upstream and downstream modules was constructed to enable MT overproduction in E. coli. The upstream plasmid pMVA1 was built on a pAC-derived backbone with spectinomycin resistance and harbors seven genes involved in the entire mevalonate pathway. The genes of EcatoB (E. coli acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase), Sahmgs, and Sahmgr (Staphylococcus aureus HMG-CoA synthase and reductase) were placed under the control of the pLac promoter (inducible by IPTG). Scmk (Saccharomyces cerevisiae BY4741 mevalonate kinase), Scpmk (S. cerevisiae phosphomevalonate kinase), Scpmd (S. cerevisiae phosphomevalonate decarboxylase), and EcIDI (E. coli isopentenyl diphosphate isomerase) were driven by the pTrc promoter (inducible by IPTG), enabling tunable flux from acetyl-CoA to IPP/DMAPP through IPTG induction with varied concentration. For the downstream biosynthetic pathway, the plasmid of pLina1+EUP, pGer1+EUP, pLav5+EUP, pNer1+EUP, pBor3+EUP, or pTerp1+EUP was constructed based on a pMB1-based backbone carrying an ampicillin resistance marker, respectively. This plasmid encodes one of three prenyl diphosphate synthases—trAgGPPS (truncated Abies grandis geranyl pyrophosphate synthase), trLiLPPS (truncated Lavandula x intermedia lavandulyl pyrophosphate synthase), or trSlNPPS (truncated Solanum lycopersicum neryl pyrophosphate synthase) under the control of a pT7 promoter (inducible by IPTG), in combination with various MTSs (Supplementary Data 5) under control of the pLux promoter that was induced by 3-oxohexanoyl-homoserine lactone (3OC6-HSL). Additionally, DpADA (Dickeya parazeae Ech586 acetaldehyde dehydrogenase) and ScADSH2 (S. cerevisiae alcohol dehydrogenase) in EUP were also included to boost the supply of acetyl-CoA using ethanol as substrate. The EUP module was driven by a constitutive promoter GryA44. Co-transformation of pMVA1 and pLina1+EUP, pGer1+EUP, pLav5+EUP_mut2, pNer1+EUP, pBor3+EUP, or pTerp1+EUP in to E. coli MG1655(DE3) ∆endA ∆recA or other derivative strains enabled the engineered strains to overproduce MTs using glycerol and/or ethanol as carbon source. The detailed plasmid and strain information is provided in Supplementary Data 7-9.

A single colony of the MT-producing strain was inoculated into 2 mL LB medium supplemented with 50 μg/mL spectinomycin and 50 μg/mL ampicillin. The culture was incubated overnight at 37 °C with shaking at 250 rpm. Subsequently, 2% (v/v) of the seed cultures were transferred into 2 mL M2 medium containing the same antibiotics. The culture was incubated at 37 °C with shaking at 250 rpm until the OD600 reached ~1.0 or ~2.0, IPTG and 3OC6-HSL were added with appropriate concentrations, overlaying with 400 μL of hexadecane for in situ product extraction. Culture fermentation was carried out at 30 °C with shaking at 250 rpm for 48 h. After the fermentation was completed, the mixture was centrifuged at 16,000 g for 5 min, and 10 μL of the obtained upper organic phase was mixed with 190 μL of ethyl acetate for GC and GC-MS analysis.

Monoculture and coculture for de novo biosynthesis of MTEs

To biosynthesize LA using a single-strain mode, LiAAT4 was employed for strain construction based on substrate pairing evaluation. The plasmid pLiAAT4K (pCDF backbone with kanamycin resistance) was constructed under the control of the pCym promoter (inducible by cumic acid) to express LiAAT4, capable of converting linalool to LA. Transformation of pLiAAT4K into the strain Lina1 yielded strain LinaA1 for LA de novo biosynthesis from glycerol and ethanol. Further optimization of IPTG, 3OC6-HSL, and cumic acid concentration was conducted to balance the pathway modules. A single colony of LinaA1 from plate was inoculated into 2 mL LB medium supplemented with 50 μg/mL spectinomycin and 50 μg/mL ampicillin. The culture was incubated overnight at 37 °C with shaking at 250 rpm. Subsequently, 2% (v/v) of the seed cultures were transferred into 2 mL M2 medium containing the same antibiotics. The culture was incubated at 37 °C with shaking at 250 rpm until the OD600 reached ~2.0, IPTG, 3OC6-HSL, and cumic acid were added with appropriate concentrations, overlaying with 400 μL of hexadecane for in situ product extraction. Culture fermentation was carried out at 30 °C with shaking at 250 rpm for 48 h. After the fermentation, the mixture was centrifuged at 16,000 g for 5 min, and 20 μL of the obtained upper organic phase was mixed with 80 μL of ethyl acetate for GC and GC-MS analysis.

To biosynthesize LA using a coculture mode, co-transformation of pLiAAT4 and pEmpty, pCaBACT+LiAAT4 and pEmpty1, or pCaBAPCT+LiAAT4 and pEup1 into E. coli MG1655(DE3) ΔendA ΔrecA ΔtnaA Δpta were conducted to obtain the strains AATE1, AATE2, and AATE3, capable of converting linalool to LA with and without CaBACT and EUP, allowing us to investigate whether maintaining CaBACT and enhancing the supply of acetyl-CoA would affect the production titer of LA. Further coculturing of linalool-producing strain Lina3 and ester-producing strain AATE3 was conducted with varying the inoculation ratio (20:1 to 1:10). For the coculture fermentation setup, single colonies of each strain were inoculated into 2 mL LB medium supplemented with 50 μg/mL spectinomycin and 50 μg/mL ampicillin. The culture was incubated overnight at 37 °C with shaking at 250 rpm. Subsequently, 2% (v/v) of the primary seed cultures were transferred into 30 mL of fresh M2 medium containing the same antibiotics in 50 mL shake flasks to prepare secondary seed cultures. Once both secondary cultures reached an OD600 of ~2.0, equal volumes (1 mL + 1 mL; inoculation ratio set as 1:1) of each culture were mixed to initiate coculture fermentation. To vary the inoculation ratio, one of the secondary seed cultures was diluted with fresh M2 medium containing the same antibiotics, after which equal volumes (1 mL + 1 mL) were combined to maintain a constant total inoculum volume. Induction was performed by adding appropriate concentrations of IPTG and 3OC6-HSL, followed by adding 10 g/L ethanol depending on the strain used and overlaying with 400 μL of hexadecane for in situ product extraction. Coculture fermentation was carried out at 30 °C and 250 rpm for 48 h. After the fermentation, the obtained upper organic phase was used for GC and GC-MS analysis.

To biosynthesize GB using a single-strain mode, FaAAT was employed for strain construction based on substrate pairing evaluation. A plasmid pFaAATK (pCDF backbone with kanamycin resistance) was constructed to coexpress FaAAT along with a butyryl-CoA biosynthetic module comprising EcatoB, Cahbd, Cacrt, and Tdter. The genes EcatoB and Cahbd were placed under the control of the pLac promoter, while Cacrt and Tdter were placed under the control of the pTrc promoter, and FaAAT was placed under the control of the pCym promoter. Transformation of pFaAATK into the strain Ger1 yielded strain GerB1 for GB de novo biosynthesis from glycerol using the single-strain mode. However, a preliminary optimization of inducer concentration did not bring a detectable titer of GB (Data not shown). To biosynthesize GB using a coculture mode, the ester-producing strain with a two-plasmid system was constructed, which contained (1) plasmid pButy1 (pAC backbone with spectinomycin resistance) carrying the butyryl-CoA biosynthetic module under the control of the T7 and trc promoter and (2) plasmid pFaAAT or pCaBACT+FaAAT (pMB1 backbone with ampicillin resistance) carrying FaAAT, with or without CaBACT under the control of the pLac promoter. Co-transformation of these two plasmids into E. coli MG1655(DE3) ΔendA ΔrecA Δpta ΔldhA ΔadhE yielded strain But1 and But2 capable of converting geraniol into GB. Subsequently, the FaAAT in pCaBACT+FaAAT was replaced with a mutant, yielding pCaBACT+F303GFaAAT and pCaBACT+I303GFaAAT2, with pButy1 co-transformed producing strains But3 and But4. Coculturing of the geraniol-producing strain Ger3 and the ester-producing strain But4 was conducted with varying the inoculation ratio (20:1 to 1:10) upon induction. After the coculture fermentation setup, the induction was performed by adding appropriate concentrations of IPTG and 3OC6-HSL, followed by overlaying with 400 μL of dodecane/hexadecane. The fermentation was conducted at 30 °C and 250 rpm for 48 h. The sample of the upper organic phase was collected for GC and GC-MS analysis.

To biosynthesize lavandulyl acetate, neryl acetate, bornyl acetate, lavandulyl butyrate, and neryl butyrate, coculture fermentation was performed using optimized MT-producing strains (Lav15, Ner3, Bor5) and inducer concentrations. Based on preliminary screening, LiAAT4 (for acetate esters) and I303GFaAAT2 (for butyrate esters) were expressed in AAT-expressing strains AATE3 and But4, respectively. Single colonies of each strain were inoculated into 2 mL LB medium supplemented with 50 μg/mL spectinomycin and 50 μg/mL ampicillin, and the culture was cultured overnight at 37 °C with shaking at 250 rpm. Then, 2% (v/v) of the seed cultures were transferred into 30 mL M2 medium with proper antibiotics in 50 mL shake flasks for secondary growth. Once the OD600 reached ~2.0, coculture was initiated by mixing the secondary cultures at an inoculation ratio of either 15:1 for lavandulyl acetate, neryl acetate, bornyl acetate biosynthesis or 1:1 for lavandulyl butyrate, neryl butyrate biosynthesis. Induction was performed by adding IPTG and 3OC6-HSL at the optimized concentrations, followed by adding 10 g/L ethanol with the strain containing the plasmid with EUP, and 400 μL hexadecane overlay for in situ product extraction. Fermentation was carried out at 30 °C and 250 rpm for 48 h. After fermentation, the hexadecane phase was collected for GC-MS analysis.

Scale-up of MTE production in a bioreactor

Fed-batch fermentations for LA and GB production were conducted in a 1-L bioreactor (BLBIO-1L, BaiLun Biotechnology Co., Ltd, Shanghai, China) containing 400 mL of M2 medium supplemented with 50 μg/mL spectinomycin and 50 μg/mL ampicillin. Single colonies of each strain used in the coculture system were inoculated into 2 mL LB medium supplemented with spectinomycin 50 μg/mL and ampicillin 50 μg/mL, and cultured overnight at 37 °C with shaking at 250 rpm. Next, two seed cultures were transferred into two independent 50 mL flasks containing 30 mL of LB medium supplemented with spectinomycin 50 μg/mL and ampicillin 50 μg/mL, and the culture was cultured for 5-7 h at 37 °C in a shaking incubator at 250 rpm. Subsequently, two seed cultures with OD600 reaching ~2 from two independent shake flasks were inoculated into the fermenter at the defined ratio (Lina3:AATE3=15:1, or Ger3:But4=1:1, v/v), and the culture temperature was set to 37 °C. The pH of fermentation broth in the bioreactor was maintained at 7.0 using 30% (v/v) ammonia solution and 30% (v/v) phosphoric acid. Air was continuously supplied at a rate of 0.4 L/min. The dissolved oxygen level was maintained at 20% by automatically adjusting the agitation speed to 300-800 rpm. Induction was initiated when the OD600 reached ~2.0 by adding 0.05 mM IPTG and 0.2 μM 3OC6-HSL for LA production, or 0.1 mM IPTG and 1 μM 3OC6-HSL for GB production. Approximately 220 mL of hexadecane for LA production or dodecane for GB production was added to capture the produced esters. After induction, the culture temperature was changed to 30 °C, and a feeding strategy was implemented every ~12 h to maintain glycerol concentration to be ~10 g/L using 600 g/L glycerol feeding medium during the entire fermentation process.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript reports the development of a dual-substrate microbial platform for the programmable biosynthesis of monoterpenoate esters (MTEs). The topic is timely and relevant to synthetic biology and enzyme engineering. Although the study contains a large amount of experimental data and presents potentially valuable ideas, the current version suffers from substantial issues in experimental logic, mechanistic interpretation, and data presentation. The central claim of establishing a “programmable and generalizable” MTE biosynthetic platform is not convincingly demonstrated, as key mechanistic and structural evidence remains incomplete. Therefore, in its current form, I do not consider the manuscript suitable for publication in Nature Communications.

Major Comments
1. Overall, the manuscript lacks conceptual coherence—for instance, the discussion of substrate tunnel determinants is not logically connected to the subsequent single-site (Phe302) mutagenesis, and several mechanistic claims rely solely on qualitative molecular dynamics observations rather than quantitative or energetic analyses. Figures and supplementary data are poorly organized, with inconsistent labeling, missing statistical information, and unclear residue numbering. In addition, undefined abbreviations, enzyme names, and inconsistent figure references further undermine readability.
2. Line 137–186: The section aims to explore the diversity of MTE biosynthesis. In Lines 144–160, the authors examined AAT-catalyzed reactions using various short-chain acyl-CoAs, whereas in Lines 162–186, only benzoic acid was used as the representative aromatic acid substrate. Please clarify the rationale for choosing benzoic acid instead of a broader set of aromatic acids. Discuss whether the platform can be generalized for MTEs derived from other aromatic acids.
3. In the first section, “Biosynthesis of monoterpenoate ester,” the catalytic capacity of AATs is demonstrated. However, the following discussion (Lines 188–213) shifts to AAT tunnel architecture and substrate specificity, whereas the subsequent section focuses again on product biosynthesis. This abrupt structural transition disrupts the logical flow. Please reassess the organization to ensure that sections follow a consistent conceptual progression.
4. In lines 200–213, The authors emphasize tunnel determinants (length, bottleneck radius, steric-gate residues) as key to substrate selectivity but subsequently target only Phe302 near the active site. Please clarify why tunnel-level mutations were not prioritized. Specifically: (1) Clarify why tunnel engineering was not prioritized; (2) If tunnel-level modification was not attempted, discuss the advantages and limitations of tunnel versus single-residue engineering, and how these approaches could be integrated; (3) Propose one or two feasible tunnel engineering schemes (e.g., multi-site substitutions near the bottleneck, tunnel expansion, or curvature modification) to demonstrate conceptual completeness and forward-looking design.
5. The current explanation for altered substrate selectivity relies mainly on geometric parameters (e.g., D2 distance from MD simulations). Interatomic distances alone cannot justify energetic or catalytic effects. To strengthen the mechanistic argument, quantitative analyses are recommended: (1) Binding free energy calculations (MMGBSA or MMPBSA): Compare the binding affinities (ΔG_bind) of acetyl-CoA and butyryl-CoA before and after mutation, and decompose the energetic components (van der Waals, electrostatics, solvation, and nonpolar terms); (2) Free energy profiling (umbrella sampling, WHAM, or metadynamics) to map the binding and reaction energy landscapes and assess whether the mutation raises the acetyl-CoA barrier.
6. The discussion on Phe302 mutations (e.g., F302G) attributes substrate selectivity changes to geometric alterations near the catalytic pocket. Docking and MD simulations, though informative, are insufficient to describe transition-state stabilization or reaction barriers. QM/MM calculations would provide quantitative insight into how these mutations reshape the catalytic energy surface and selectivity, and are strongly encouraged.
7. Line 380: The statement “For GPP-derived MTs, the titers obtained were varied when MTPS was changed” lacks definition and mechanistic explanation. Please define MTPS, describe how its variation affects MTE titers, and provide the corresponding quantitative data, as this relationship is not evident in Supplementary Fig. 46b–e.
8. Lines 364–386: This section describes de novo biosynthesis of six distinct MTs involving four modules: the mevalonate (MVA) module, downstream MVA module, PDPS module, and MTS module. However, these modules are not clearly delineated in the metabolic schematic (Supplementary Fig. 46a). Please redraw or reorganize the figure into clearly labeled modules to enhance interpretability.

Minor Comments
1.In the first section “Biosynthesis of monoterpenoate ester,” Fig. 2d, which demonstrates AAT catalytic capability, is difficult for readers to interpret. Please consider presenting this data using a clearer schematic or a tabular format to improve readability.
2.Line 199: The text refers to residue Phe299, but Supplementary Fig. 26d shows only Phe309. Please verify and correct the numbering.
3.Line 276: Residues Gly162 and Ser378 mentioned in the text do not correspond to those in Supplementary Fig. 32a (which shows G160 and S377). Please ensure residue numbering consistency throughout the manuscript.
4.Line 280: The term “NDT mutagenesis” appears for the first time without being spelled out. Please provide the full name upon first mention.
5.Line 284: The abbreviations GA titer and GB titer appear without full definitions. Please define them at first occurrence.
6.Line 310: The SDS-PAGE image in Supplementary Fig. 36a does not clearly show the claimed “poor soluble expression of both wtFaAAT and F302GFaAAT.” Please provide a higher-resolution image or a clearer version of the gel.
7.In both the main text and Supplementary Information, the x-axis labels of Supplementary Figs. 32b–e are unclear. Please clarify the axis descriptions or revise the figures.
8.When describing the effect of the F302G mutation, several statements are overly qualitative (e.g., “significantly reduced acetyl-CoA catalytic efficiency”). Quantitative data such as the exact fold-change or kinetic parameters (kcat, Km, kcat/Km) should be provided.
