## Paper

## Abstract

Reconstructing the precise biosynthesis of structurally complex natural esters, such as monoterpene esters, in engineered microbes remains a major challenge, owing to the limited repertoire of highly selective alcohol acyltransferases and the lack of compatible pathway modularity. Here, we establish a dual-substrate microbial platform to profile the activities of alcohol acyltransferase (AAT) to synthesize three distinct classes of monoterpene esters: monoterpenyl esters, monoterpenoate esters, and monoterpenyl monoterpenoate esters, enabling access to both natural and non-natural monoterpene ester biosynthetic pathways. Through structure-guided critical residue engineering and dual-substrate molar ratio tuning, we achieve selective biosynthesis of >C2 acyl-CoA-derived monoterpene esters, despite competing intracellular acetyl-CoA. Coculture engineering further redistributed metabolic fluxes between acyl-CoA and alcohol precursors, yielding 11.50 g/L linalyl acetate and 3.16 g/L geranyl butyrate in 1-L bioreactor. This study expands the biosynthetic space of monoterpene esters and provides a versatile strategy to control AAT selectivity, offering a plug-and-play, scalable framework for ester biomanufacturing.

---

## Introduction

Natural esters, primarily recognized as either volatile compounds responsible for fruity and floral aromas or as acylated derivatives of complex natural products, are ubiquitous in flowers, traditional fermented foods, and medicinal plants (e.g., rose1, 2, wine3, Baijiu4, Strychnos nux-vomica5, etc). Since the term "ester" was first introduced in 1848 by German chemist Leopold Gmelin to describe the condensation product of acids and alcohols6, natural esters have garnered extensive attention due to their structural diversity, sensory importance, and biosynthetic complexity. Their entire biosynthesis involves intricate modular biosynthetic pathways distributed across microbial and plant cellular systems4, 7. Engineering microbes to synthesize these esters presents considerable challenges, particularly in achieving controlled and efficient biosynthetic pathways. A primary hurdle is the unclear specificity and selectivity of enzymes at critical metabolic junctions8. Natural ester intracellular biosynthesis is predominantly mediated by alcohol acyltransferases (AATs), which catalyze the esterification of acyl-CoAs and alcohols9. However, the inherent broad substrate promiscuities of AATs for both donor dimensions typically form multiple ester products instead of the desired singular compound in engineered microbial or natural systems10. Furthermore, intracellular ester biosynthesis relies heavily on the availability of dual substrates—acyl-CoAs and alcohols—whose availability is regulated by primary or secondary metabolic networks11, 12, such as glycolysis, citric acid cycle, fatty acid biosynthesis/degradation, amino acid biosynthesis/degradation, mevalonate pathway, polyketide biosynthesis, etc. Typically, the imbalance or limitation in precursor supply from these upstream biosynthetic pathways, whether in nature or engineered hosts, can critically hinder AAT-driven ester formation, thereby reducing product formation specificity and efficiency.

Over the past two decades, advancements in metabolic engineering have significantly facilitated microbial design, enabling AAT-mediated biosynthesis of structurally diverse esters using engineered microbes consuming glucose, glycerol, or ethanol13-16. Ester biosynthesis approaches in engineered microbes have involved esterification of short-chain fatty alcohols (SCFAlcs) with various acyl-CoAs by AATs17, optimization of enzyme specificity through substrate-tunnel engineering to reduce intermediate-derived by-product formation7, and coculture strategies to minimize cellular metabolic burdens and substrate promiscuity by dissecting the entire biosynthetic pathway and temporally cascade inoculations18. Despite these progressions, precision ester biosynthesis in engineered microbes remains constrained by insufficiently characterized biocatalytic modules of AATs and the incompatibility of upstream metabolic pathways17, 19-21.

Monoterpene esters (MEs), a highly valuable class of natural products extensively applied as flavors, fragrances, food additives, cosmetic ingredients, advanced biofuels, insecticides, etc (Supplementary Tables 1-2, Supplementary Data 1)9, 22-26, exemplify these constraints in microbial biosynthesis. Structurally, MEs originate primarily from the esterifying reactions between monoterpenols (MTs) and acyl donors, or between alcohols and monoterpenoic acid (MTa)-derived acyl-CoAs (Fig. 1). However, current engineered microbial systems produce a narrow range of MEs, primarily derived from acetyl-CoA27, including geranyl acetate (GAC)28, neryl acetate29, and perilla acetate30. Controlling the specificity of ME biosynthesis critically depends on the characterization and development of highly selective AATs capable of utilizing C>2 acyl-CoAs amid high intracellular acetyl-CoA concentrations. Moreover, as both monoterpenes and acyl-CoAs share acetyl-CoA as a common precursor, finely tuning the molar ratio and compatibility of metabolic fluxes toward alcohol and acyl-CoA biosynthesis is essential to achieve high specificity and titer of ME in engineered microbes.

Here, we develop a dual-substrate microbial platform to profile the catalytic activities of AATs in engineered Escherichia coli, synthesizing three distinct classes of MEs: Monoterpenyl Esters (MTEs), Monoterpenoate Esters (MTaEs), and Monoterpenyl Monoterpenoate Esters (MtMtaEs) (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1). By bioconverting MTs or MTas individually with their pairing substrates, we generate 64 MTEs, 3 MTaEs, and 4 MtMtaEs, a type of underexplored monoterpene dimeric esters with four isoprene units. This comprehensive profiling enables the identification of AAT exhibiting either broad or highly specific dual-substrate acceptance patterns for both alcohols and acyl-CoAs. Structure-guided engineering of the critical residue in AATs under adjusted acyl-CoA-to-alcohol molar ratios efficiently mitigated substrate specificity imbalances, in particular between acetyl-CoA and butyryl-CoA, allowing the precise biosynthesis of a variety of MEs and aromatic esters with >99% selectivity. Leveraging a modular coculture strategy to enhance dual-substrate availability and compatibility, we demonstrate the de novo biosynthesis of 7 MTEs using an E. coli-E. coli consortium with MT as the bridging molecule, achieving a titer exceeding 11 g/L for one MTE in a 1-liter bioreactor. This study highlights the advantages of AAT-mediated ME biosynthesis and provides a versatile framework for selective ester biosynthesis in engineered microbes, significantly enhancing the diversity, substrate specificity, and pathway modularity.

---

## Results

Biosynthesis of monoterpenoate esters

To explore the diversity of MTE biosynthesis using various sourced AATs, the acid donor should be available as CoA-activated molecules (Fig. 2a). We selected a butyrate-acetoacetate CoA-transferase from Clostridium acetobutylicum (CaBACT) for activating short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) into acyl-CoAs31. The selection of the 14 AATs from bacteria, yeast, and plant was based on the previously reported studies, indicating their enzymatic activity in forming acetate-based MTEs7, 19, 32, 33. The phylogenetic analysis reveals the evolutionary divergence and conservation among the amino acid sequences of AATs (Fig. 2b and 2c, Supplementary Fig. 2). The close clustering of LiAAT4, FvAAT, and FaAAT in the phylogenetic tree suggests that these AATs may share a similar dual-substrate specificity. Using engineered E. coli strains expressing individual AATs with or without CaBACT, we conducted esterification reactions by feeding selected MTs and carboxylic acids. The resulting MTEs were captured into the organic phase of culture during fermentation and analyzed by GC-MS (Supplementary Fig. 3). Characteristic ester bond fragmentation patterns were observed, with monoterpenols such as geraniol, nerol, and lavandulol forming base ions at m/z = 69 and linalool at m/z = 93 due to its distinct allylic rearrangement (Supplementary Table 3)34. Characteristic m/z fragments (43, 57, 71, 85) derived from C2-C5 SCFAs enabled unambiguous MTE identification, even without NIST MS references (Supplementary Data 2). Four representative AATs, including FvAAT, FaAAT, LiAAT4, and ScAAT1, were characterized for their activities with acetyl-CoA, propionyl-CoA, and valeryl-CoA. FvAAT, FaAAT, and LiAAT4 displayed broad catalytic activity, capable of accepting C2-C5 acyl donors and diverse MTs (Fig. 2d, Supplementary Figs. 4-25). Among all the validated AATs, LiAAT4 and ScAAT1 showed catalytic activity toward primary-to-tertiary MTs (Fig. 2d).

To activate aromatic acids into their respective acyl-CoAs, we constructed the plasmids harboring the genes coding for an individual AAT with an ATP-dependent fatty/aromatic acid-CoA ligase (ACSL) from Thauera terpenica (TtLACSL)35, Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1 (PaLACSL)36, or ATP-dependent benzoate-CoA ligase from Hypericum (HzBCL)37. A preliminary experiment revealed that only TtLACSL exhibited benzoate-CoA activation activity when benzoate and geraniol were co-fed to the strains co-expressing individual ACSL or BCL with FaAAT. We then constructed strains with plasmids co-expressing TtLACSL with various AATs for further evaluation. In addition to FvAAT, FaAAT, LiAAT4, and ScAAT1, we validated three benzyl alcohol O-benzoyltransferases (BABTs) to assess their activities on aromatic acid-derived MTE formation. PhBABT was previously reported to esterify aromatic acid-derived acyl-CoAs with linalool and geraniol38. Identified via BLAST with ≥70% sequence identity to PhBABT in NCBI protein database, we included two additional BABTs (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Fig. 2). The evaluation indicated that FvAAT, FaAAT, and PmBABT produced the corresponding benzoate MTEs (Fig. 2d, Supplementary Figs. 4-25). FvAAT and FaAAT exhibited a wide range of substrate specificity for various MTs for benzoyl-CoA-derived MTEs, which are widely used in the flavor, fragrance, and cosmetic industries, where they contribute sweet, floral, and fruity notes39. PmBABT showed better catalytic activity for the accessed MTs and could exclusively generate benzoate MTEs (e.g., lavandulyl benzoate, geranyl benzoate, neryl benzoate, and perillyl benzoate, Fig. 2d, Supplementary Figs. 7, 9, 11, and 13). Building on these findings, we profiled the capacity of FvAAT and FaAAT to form phenylacetyl-CoA- and phenylpropionyl-CoA-derived MTEs. The identification shows that FaAAT possesses broad catalytic activities for esterifying aromatic acid-derived acyl-CoA with multiple MTs (Fig. 2d, Supplementary Figs. 4-25).

Biosynthesis of monoterpenoate and monoterpenyl monoterpenoate ester

Primary MTs, in plant or microbe, would undergo oxidation to form corresponding MTas, typically mediated by two sequential steps conduct using alcohol dehydrogenases40, 41. We hypothesized that the activation of MTa with HS-CoA by TtLACSL would possibly form monoterpenoyl-CoA, which can be subsequently esterified with SCFAlcs into MTaE (Fig. 3a). This design enables the expansion of microbial ME diversity by leveraging AAT promiscuity towards underexplored dual-substrate reactions. We evaluated the activities of FvAAT, FaAAT, LiAAT4, ScAAT1, ScEEB1, ScEHT1-1, ScEHT1-2, PmBABT, MsBABT, and PhBABT, to form MTaTE (Fig. 3b, the last three were not shown in the figure as no product was detected). By pairing two MTas with three SCFAlcs for the bioconversion, the analysis of the formed compounds in the organic phase using GC-MS showed that (S)-(-)-perillic acid was successfully activated with HS-CoA by TtLACSL and esterified by FaAAT, LiAAT4, and ScEHT1-2 into three respective MTaEs, namely ethyl (S)-(-)-perillate, propyl (S)-(-)-perillate, and butyl (S)-(-)-perillate (Fig. 3b-d). The fragmentation of these MTaEs during ionization would generate a base peak of (S)-(-)-perillic acid with an m/z = 121 (Supplementary Table 4), and characterization of these bioconversion-produced MTaEs was verified by mass spectrometry using the NMR-confirmed, chemically synthesized standards as references (Supplementary Figs. 26-28). As such, incorporating the MTaEs biosynthesized here into the ME family demonstrates the capacity to harness the promiscuity of plant-derived AATs for diversifying natural and non-natural ME biosynthesis.

The conceptual visualization of the dual-substrate ME biosynthesis inspired us to explore the biosynthesis of the third type of MEs (Fig. 1). Theoretically, monoterpenoyl-CoA activated from MTa and HS-CoA could undergo esterification by AATs using either structurally homo- or hetero-type MTs as alcohol donors, resulting in the formation of MtMtaEs (Fig. 3e). Although MtMtaE consists of four isoprene units and shares the same carbon count (C20) with canonical diterpenes, they are structurally distinct as they are not synthesized via the geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate pathway. We paired and co-fed 11 MTs with two MTas into the medium to explore the possibility of MtMtaE formation by FvAAT, FaAAT, LiAAT4, ScAAT1, ScEHT1-2, PmBABET, MsBABT, and PhBABT (Fig. 3f, the last three were not shown in the figure as no product was detected). The analysis of the compounds formed in the organic phase using GC-MS revealed that both geranic acid and (S)-(-)-perillic acid could be activated by TtLACSL to their CoA molecules, which were esterified by FaAAT into four respective MtMtaEs (Fig. 3g-i). The base peaks of geranic acid and (S)-(-)-perillic acid would be m/z =69 and 121, respectively (Supplementary Table 4). The characterization of these bioconversion-produced MtMtaEs was verified by mass spectrometry with the NMR-confirmed, chemically synthesized standards as references (Supplementary Figs. 29-31). MtMtaEs represent a unique class of monoterpene dimers with the molecular formula C20H30O2, previously detected in atmospheric secondary organic aerosols42, yet their biosynthetic origins in living organisms remain largely unexplored. The dual-substrate microbial platform accelerates the discovery and characterization of MtMtaEs, offering a viable method for biosynthesizing monoterpene dimeric esters. Importantly, the conversion of volatile and membrane-permeable monoterpenes into bulkier MtMtaEs alters their physicochemical properties, reducing volatility while favoring sequestration in subcellular storage compartments such as lipid droplets or peroxisomes. Such compartmentalization not only possibly alleviates product toxicity but also establishes a stable reservoir that supports more efficient and sustainable monoterpene biosynthesis.

Reprogramming AAT selectivity via single-residue mutagenesis and dual-substrate ratio

We performed molecular docking of the AlphaFold2-predicted FaAAT, LiAAT4, FvAAT, and PmBABT in complex with acyl-CoAs, revealing distinct differences in active-site organization that underlie their distinct substrate preferences (Supplementary Fig. 32). Although these AATs share a conserved acyl-CoA binding framework coordinated by key catalytic residues (e.g., His and Asp), the composition and geometry of the acyl-binding pocket vary substantially. FaAAT and FvAAT, which preferentially accept short-chain acyl donors, possess relatively narrow and hydrophobic acyl pockets shaped by residues such as Ala/Val and Phe/Leu, forming a compact environment around acetyl-CoA (Supplementary Fig. 32a-b). In contrast, LiAAT4 exhibits a more restricted cavity due to substitution by bulkier residues (e.g., Tyr), whereas PmBABT displays a distinct adaptation for aromatic substrates, with benzoyl-CoA stabilized by expanded hydrophobic contacts and additional polar interactions (Supplementary Fig. 32c-d). Consistent with these pocket-level differences, substrate tunnel architectures across these AATs differ in length, bottleneck radius, and residue composition (Supplementary Fig. 33). FaAAT and FvAAT feature extended tunnels that can accommodate elongated aliphatic substrates, whereas PmBABT exhibits shorter and more constrained pathways. These global tunnel features rationalize broad differences in substrate scope among AATs; however, they primarily govern substrate accessibility rather than fine discrimination between structurally similar acyl donors. In particular, the precise selectivity of FaAAT toward acetyl- versus butyryl-CoA cannot be explained by tunnel geometry alone, implicating localized interactions and dynamic effects near the catalytic center.

Accordingly, we focused on FaAAT to further investigate how ligand-binding residues govern acetyl-CoA versus butyryl-CoA selectivity using geraniol as a fixed alcohol donor. Molecular docking using the AlphaFold2-predicted FaAAT suggested that acyl-CoA binds within a shared pocket adjacent to the catalytic residue His157, with 303Phe, 162Gly, 250His, 378Ser, and 380Trp located in close proximity to the acyl-CoA moiety (Supplementary Fig. 34). Among them, 303Phe was proposed as a key residue proximal to 157His that influences the relative binding geometry of C2 and C4 acyl-CoAs to geraniol (Fig. 4a-b, Supplementary Fig. 34a). To test this hypothesis, structure-guided NDT codon-based saturation mutagenesis (N = A/C/G/T, D = A/G/T, T = thymine) was performed. Several variants exhibited selectively enhanced on butyryl-CoA over acetyl-CoA (Supplementary Fig. 34b-f). Replacement of 303Phe with small side-chain residues (e.g., Gly, Ser, and Asn) significantly reduced GA formation without causing a substantial decrease in geranyl butyrate (GB) titer. Additional substitutions at G162, H250, S378, and W380 on F303GFaAAT did not yield further improvements in selectivity or product titer (Supplementary Fig. 35), indicating that, for short-chain acyl-CoA discrimination in FaAAT, double-site tunnel reshaping is less effective than localized residue engineering near the catalytic center, likely as excessive tunnel perturbation compromises productive acyl-CoA positioning.

Phylogenetic analysis revealed substantial diversity among plant-derived AATs; however, a conserved aromatic or bulky aliphatic residue (Tyr, Phe, or Ile) is frequently observed at position 303 (Fig. 4c, Supplementary Fig. 36). Furthermore, mutagenesis at position 303 in FaAAT resulted in substrate-dependent changes in the production profiles of MTaEs and MtMtaEs (Supplementary Fig. 37), indicating that this residue influences acyl-donor preference beyond the geraniol-based system.

Representative poses of acetyl-CoA-geraniol and butyryl-CoA-geraniol complexes generated from the AlphaFold2-predicted F303GFaAAT revealed altered substrate orientations and contact patterns in the vicinity of the active site after mutation (Fig. 4d-e). However, because molecular docking provides only static and non-unique binding hypotheses, we then examined mutation-induced effects using pre-reaction state (PRS) molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. These analyses revealed that the F303G mutation does not uniformly shorten substrate contact distances but instead redistributes dynamic interaction patterns within the acyl-CoA thioester environment, particularly involving 284Asn and 378Ser, in a substrate-dependent manner (Supplementary Fig. 38). Moreover, comparative perturbation response scanning molecular dynamics (PRS-MD) analyses revealed that homologous mutations in closely related FaAAT2 can modulate distinct reaction coordinates. In FaAAT, the F303G mutation primarily reshapes thioester torsional conformations, whereas in FaAAT2 with an isoleucine at the corresponding position, the analogous I303G mutation in FaAAT2 alters the Bürgi-Dunitz attack geometry. This divergence indicates that mutation-induced selectivity arises from enzyme-specific reorganization of reactive conformational ensembles rather than static distance changes alone (Supplementary Fig. 39).

The intracellular availability of acyl-CoA and MT affects the apparent specificity of dual-substrate esterification catalyzed by AATs, which can be modulated by varying the molar ratio of the substrates. To confirm this, we profiled the formations of GB and GA at varying dual-substrate molar ratios, both wtFaAAT and F303GFaAAT exhibited high exponential curve fitting confidence for GA and GB formation (R2>0.99, Fig. 4f, Supplementary Data 3, No. 31-34). The selectivity for GLB formation was improved at all tested dual-substrate molar ratios (Fig. 4g). The strain harboring F303GFaAAT achieved a GB selectivity of 98.95% under a 4:1 butyrate-to-geraniol molar ratio, representing a 3.12-fold (p < 0.001) increase relative to wtFaAAT under a 1:4 ratio; even under 1:4 butyrate-to-geraniol molar ratio, F303GFaAAT still exhibited a 2.21-fold improvement in GB selectivity compared with wtFaAAT (p < 0.001; Fig. 4g). Consistent with this trend, the other two beneficial substitutions at position 303 of FaAAT also showed improved GB selectivity under higher butyrate-to-geraniol ratios (Supplementary Fig. 34g-i).

To elucidate the enzymatic basis underlying these mutation-enhanced selectivity effects, we next characterized the intrinsic catalytic properties of wtFaAAT and F303GFaAAT in vitro. The F303G mutation in FaAAT resulted in no detectable product in the acetyl-CoA/geraniol reaction, indicating a loss of enzyme catalytic activity toward acetyl-CoA upon introduction of the F303G mutation under the tested conditions in vitro (Fig. 4h, Supplementary Figs. 40-41). In contrast, for the butyryl-CoA/geraniol reaction, quantitative kinetic analysis was feasible. The Km value showed no significant change upon mutation (1.04-fold difference relative to the wild type, p = 0.66), indicating that substrate binding affinity for butyryl-CoA was largely preserved. However, the catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) was significantly reduced to 0.35-fold of wtFaAAT (p < 0.001) (Fig. 4h, Supplementary Fig. 40). These kinetics are consistent with mutation-induced destabilization of catalytically productive acetyl-CoA conformations, arising from altered local hydrogen-bonding networks involving 284Asn and 378Ser, while largely preserving butyryl-CoA binding (Supplementary Fig. 42).

Despite the favorable shift in acyl-donor preference conferred by the F303G mutation in FaAAT, the overall catalytic performance of FaAAT remained constrained under cellular conditions, prompting us to examine whether enzyme solubility represents an additional limiting factor. We observed poor soluble expression of both wtFaAAT and F303GFaAAT (Supplementary Fig. 40a), which likely caused the reduced catalytic activity for GB formation (Fig. 4f and 4i). Phylogenetic analysis and pairwise sequence alignment revealed that FaAAT2, identified from the NCBI protein database (Supplementary Fig. 40b-c), contains an Ile at position 303 and differs from FaAAT by five amino acid residues (Supplementary Fig. 36), showing improved solubility compared with FaAAT (Supplementary Fig. 40d). Profiling GB and GA production by the strains expressing wtFaAAT2 and I303GFaAAT2 varying molar ratios of butyrate-to-geraniol generated high-confidence exponential curve fitting (Supplementary Fig. 43, R²>0.98, Supplementary Data 3, No. 39-42) and a GB titer (Fig. 4i) approaching the theoretical yield (1.45 g/L, Supplementary Fig. 44). The GB selectivity achieved by the strain harboring I303GFaAAT2 (97.62%) was slightly lower than that of F303GFaAAT under a 4:1 molar ratio of butyrate-to-geraniol, but still represented a 4.22-fold increase compared to wtFaAAT2 under 1:4 molar ratio of butyrate-to-geraniol (p < 0.001) (Fig. 4j). The enhanced GB selectivity observed with I303GFaAAT2 was consistent with altered catalytic behavior, as confirmed by steady-state kinetic assays (Fig. 4k, Supplementary Fig. 40e-f), which suggests that, in FaAAT2, the apparent acyl-CoA selectivity is governed by a combined contribution of catalytic turnover, enzyme solubility, and global active-site interaction networks (Supplementary Fig. 45), rather than being solely dictated by local acyl-CoA binding energetics.

To place these enzyme determinants within a unified catalytic framework, we next examined the intrinsic reaction mechanism shared by AAT and its variants. The kinetic data are consistent with a sequential bi-bi mechanism for AAT and its variants under the tested conditions, in which geraniol and acyl-CoA form a catalytically competent ternary complex (Fig. 4I, Supplementary Fig. 46-47). To quantitatively address the catalytic mechanism, we have performed ab initio QM calculations on an enzyme model that encompasses the core reaction center (157His in FaAAT, geraniol, and CoA thioester, Supplementary Fig. 48). This model confirms the proposed mechanism: 157His facilitates geraniol deprotonation followed by nucleophilic attack on the thioester carbonyl, with a rate-determining barrier of 17.6 kcal/mol (ΔHǂ). Notably, the subsequent proton transfer from the imidazolium to thiolate is essentially barrierless, and the overall reaction is slightly exergonic (ΔG = -3.1 kcal/mol). The computed energy profile aligns well with the mechanistic scheme in Fig. 4I, suggesting the critical role of pre-organized active-site architecture in transition-state stabilization. Building on this mechanistic understanding, to validate the combined strategy of single-residue engineering and dual-substrate ratio control for precision ester biosynthesis, we characterized more substrate pairings: butyryl-CoA with nerol, butanol, and benzyl alcohol; geraniol with propionyl-CoA and benzoyl-CoA; and benzoyl-CoA with benzoyl-CoA. Exponential fittings of the product titers on the selected dual-substrate molar ratio showed high confidence (average R²>0.98 across all dual-substrate pairings (Supplementary Data 3, No. 1-30, 47-72). Modulating molar ratios of acyl-CoA-to-alcohol from 4:1 to 1:4 with varied wtAAT and its mutants significantly enhanced selectivity by 3.71-fold (neryl butyrate, p < 0.001), 1.94-fold (butyl butyrate, p < 0.001), 3.19-fold (benzyl butyrate, p < 0.001), 2.10-fold (geranyl propionate, p < 0.001), 60.13-fold (geranyl benzoate, p < 0.001), and 1.37-fold (benzyl benzoate, p < 0.001) (Supplementary Figs. 49-54), outperforming the reported AATs under comparable conditions (Supplementary Fig. 44). These results support that dual-substrate molar ratio modulation adjusts the apparent AAT selectivity, while critical residue engineering alters the AAT’s intrinsic specificity, both of which aided precision ester biosynthesis.

Coculture to de novo monoterpenoate ester biosynthesis

Connecting isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) plus dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP) or only two DMAPPs generates various prenyl diphosphate (PDSP) by PDP synthase (PDPS). Subsequent releasing diphosphate from PDP by MT synthase (MTS) would form corresponding MTs (Supplementary Fig. 55a)24. To establish de novo MT biosynthetic route from glycerol in E. coli, six representative MTs were selected—linalool, geraniol, α-terpineol, borneol, nerol, and lavandulol—covering primary, secondary, and tertiary MTs. The entire biosynthetic pathway was modularly assembled with four units: an upstream mevalonate (MVA) module, a downstream MVA module, a PDPS module, and an MTS module. Each module operon-related gene was placed under the control of two inducible promoters, enabling fine-tuned flux regulation (Supplementary Fig. 56-61). Systematic metabolic engineering revealed several key strategies to enhance MT production: increasing acetyl-CoA availability through the ethanol utilization pathway (EUP)43, 44, optimizing gene expression across modules to balance pathway flux, and reducing by-product formation via targeted gene deletions (Supplementary Fig. 55b-g, Supplementary Figs. 56-61). For GPP-derived MTs, changing MTSs in the downstream biosynthetic pathway resulted in evident differences in product titers (Supplementary Fig. 55b-e). Under optimized strain and induction conditions, the titers of linalool, geraniol, α-terpineol, borneol, and nerol reached 3.33 g/L, 1.18 g/L, 198.98 mg/L, 3.84 mg/L, and 224.42 mg/L, respectively. The titer of linalool achieved was 16.74-fold higher (p < 0.001) than that of α-terpineol. This disparity is attributable to differences among MTSs in both catalytic efficiency toward GPP and effective expression levels24, resulting in varied production titers of MTs. Besides, protein engineering of MTS to enhance their activities was therefore critical for improving MT biosynthesis. In lavandulol biosynthesis, we screened a panel of E. coli endogenous phosphatases and identified EcRdgB as the most active enzyme toward lavandulyl pyrophosphate. We further performed structure-guided multiple-round single-site mutagenesis to enhance its catalytic efficiency, obtaining the engineered variant F118D-H182CEcRdgB, which significantly improved the hydrolysis of lavandulyl pyrophosphate and consequently increased the lavandulol titer by 7.64-fold (p < 0.001) (Supplementary Fig. 61).

Inspired by the modularity of acyl-CoA and MT biosynthetic pathways in nature, we constructed a MT-producing strain and an ester-producing strain for coculture engineering (Supplementary Fig. 62a). This strategy simplifies the genetic manipulation cycle and alleviates metabolic competition for shared precursors such as acetyl-CoA45. By combining the above MT-producing strains with an esterification module containing AATs with defined substrate specificity, we produced natural linalyl acetate (LA) and GB via microbial biosynthesis. LA and GB have high industrial relevance: LA is the dominant high-value fragrance component in lavender essential oil and is widely used in perfumery, while GB is a commercially important fruity/floral flavor compound used in food, beverage, and fragrance formulations27, 46. Besides, their biosynthetic precursors—linalool and geraniol—are among the monoterpene alcohols with the higher achievable microbial titers in this study and other extensive studies, enabling a representative demonstration of MTEs biosynthesis. For acetate MTE biosynthesis using a single strain, introducing an additional plasmid overexpressing LiAAT4 with an inducible promoter into the linalool-producing strain would be achieved. However, even under optimized induction conditions, the highest titer of LA reached 0.058 g/L by the single-strain mode (Fig. 5a-b, Supplementary Fig. 63). We cocultured the linalool-producing strain with the ester-producing strain containing LiAAT4 (Fig. 5c) and optimized the critical parameters. Optimization of inoculation ratio at the induction stage, coupled with EUP module integration into the ester-producing strain, substantially enhanced LA production (Supplementary Fig. 63), achieving a titer of 3.22 g/L, representing a 55.2-fold improvement over monoculture systems (p < 0.001) (Fig. 5b). Next, to construct a single-strain system for GB production, we transformed the third plasmid with the genes coding the enzymes of butyryl-CoA biosynthetic pathway47 and wtFaAAT into the geraniol-producing strain (Fig. 5d, Supplementary Fig. 64). However, this three-plasmid-containing strain did not give a detectable titer of GB after optimizing the induction conditions for pathway balancing (Fig. 5e). We subsequently cocultured a geraniol-producing strain and a strain with butyryl-CoA biosynthetic pathway and wtFaAAT, which produced 0.077 g/L of GB (Fig. 5e-f). Because wtFaAAT provided a consistent baseline for optimizing coculture conditions, we subsequently replaced it with F303GFaAAT and I303GFaAAT2 in the ester-producing strain, which increased the GB titer to 0.32 g/L with a selectivity of 97.81% (Fig. 5e, Supplementary Fig. 64). We further expanded the product profile to biosynthesize acetate and butyrate MTEPs from glycerol using coculture strategy, and achieved the titers of lavandulyl acetate, neryl acetate, bornyl acetate, lavandulyl butyrate, and neryl butyrate to 94.49, 197.12, 2.40, 8.72, and 65.72 mg/L (Fig. 5g-k, Supplementary Fig. 62b-f).

To scale up the coculture process for ME biosynthesis, we ran fed-batch fermentation in a 1-liter bioreactor. A titer of 11.50 g/L LA was obtained, with 0.11 g/L linalool residing after 96h fermentation (Fig. 5l). Chiral column analysis of the fermenter samples confirmed the stereoselective biosynthesis of R-(–)-LA in enantiopure form, in contrast to chemically synthesized racemic LA (RS-mixture, Supplementary Fig. 62g). The GB-producing coculture reached a titer of 3.16 g/L, with 0.033 g/L GA and 0.046 g/L geraniol accumulated after 83 h, corresponding to a GB selectivity of 98.97% (Fig. 5m). Importantly, GB was obtained as an isomerically pure compound, whereas chemically synthesized standards consisted of mixed isomers including neryl butyrate (Supplementary Fig. 62h). In both cases, the target esters were captured in situ by an overlaying organic phase, which enabled efficient product partitioning from the aqueous broth and visual accumulation of ester-rich layers for further downstream purification (Fig. 5n and 5o). These results highlight the scalability, specificity, and stereochemical fidelity of the coculture strategy for de novo biosynthesis of MEs.
